sec: Secretary’s Message · ¶2
text: All who use our streets, roads and highways must follow and understand the rules of the road. Whether driving a car, motorcycle, commercial vehicle or riding a bicycle, it is critical we adhere to the rules to share the road safely and responsibly.

Always buckle up, follow traffic laws, pay attention to other drivers, bicyclists and pedestrians, and put down that cell phone when behind the wheel or handlebars. Do not operate a vehicle, motorcycle or bicycle while distracted or impaired—it could mean the difference between life and death.

Driver’s License Tests · ¶1
text: Here is an overview of the driver’s license tests:

sec: Driver’s License Tests · item 1
text: Vision Test DMV tests all applicants to ensure they can see well enough to drive safely. If you take your vision test with corrective or contact lenses, your driver’s license will have a corrective lenses restriction. If you do not pass your vision test, you will be asked to have your eye doctor complete a Report of Vision Examination (DL 62) form. For more information, visit dmv.ca.gov/vision-standards .

sec: Driver’s License Tests · item 2
text: Knowledge Test When you apply for an original driver’s license, you must pass a knowledge test with multiple choice questions. You are allowed three attempts to pass before you must reapply. Minors must wait seven days to retake a failed knowledge test, not including the day of the failure. When renewing your driver’s license, eLearning may be an alternative testing option. This is a no-fail, self-paced interactive modulated course with quizzes after each module. The course can be taken on a computer, laptop, tablet, or mobile device. Testing options will be available once you complete your application at dmv.ca.gov/dl . Important You are not allowed to use any testing aids during knowledge tests, such as a California Driver’s Handbook or cell phone.

sec: Driver’s License Tests · item 3
text: Behind-the-Wheel Drive Test When you apply for an original driver’s license, you will be tested on your ability to safely drive a vehicle. Upon renewal, drivers with a vision or medical condition may be required to take a behind-the-wheel test. The examiner may give two or more instructions at one time to determine whether you can understand and properly follow both directions. For example, “At the next street, make a left turn, and then at the first intersection make another left turn.” Visit dmv.ca.gov/make-an-appointment to schedule a behind-the-wheel drive test appointment.

sec: Other Things to Know for Your Behind-the-Wheel Test · ¶1
path: Other Things to Know for Your Behind-the-Wheel Test
text: The drive test is intended to determine your skill in operating a motor vehicle in most road situations and evaluate your abilities, not the vehicle’s technology. Therefore, advanced driver assistance systems technologies, such as automated parallel parking, lane departure, and adaptive cruise control, are not permitted during the drive test. Vehicle safety technology, such as backup cameras and blind spot monitors, may be used on the drive test, but are not a replacement for an actual visual check of your mirrors and blind spots.

sec: Intro · ¶1
text: Your health may affect your driving.

sec: Intro · ¶2
text: Vision – You must be able to notice hazards in different types of lighting, judge distances, adjust to traffic speed, and read road signs.

sec: Intro · ¶3
text: Hearing – You must be able to hear horns, sirens, motorcycles, or screeching tires that may alert you of hazards. It is illegal to wear a headset or earplugs in both ears while driving.

sec: Intro · ¶4
text: Fatigue and Drowsiness – Can affect your vision and increase reaction time to hazards.

sec: Intro · ¶5
text: Physical and Mental – You must be alert to quickly decide the correct course of action in any type of traffic situation, including unexpected ones.

sec: Intro · ¶6
text: Medications – Prescription and over-the-counter medications can make you an unsafe driver. Some medicines can make you sleepy. It is your responsibility to know the effects of the medications you take.

sec: Intro · ¶7
text: Health – Physicians are required to report patients, who are at least 14 years old, to DMV for medical conditions that may affect your ability to drive safely, such as lapse of consciousness.

text: To control your vehicle, it is critical to keep both hands on the wheel whenever possible.

sec: Controlling the Vehicle › Hand-to-Hand Steering (Push/Pull) · item 2
text: Do not cross your hands over the middle of the steering wheel.

sec: Controlling the Vehicle › Hand-to-Hand Steering (Push/Pull) · item 3

sec: Controlling the Vehicle › Hand-Over-Hand Steering · ¶1
text: Use this steering wheel method when you turn at low speeds, park, or need to recover from a skid. To use this method:

sec: Controlling the Vehicle › Hand-Over-Hand Steering · item 1
text: Start with your hands at 8 and 4 o’clock.

sec: Controlling the Vehicle › Hand-Over-Hand Steering · item 2
text: Reach across the steering wheel to grasp the opposite side.

sec: Controlling the Vehicle › Hand-Over-Hand Steering · item 3
text: Let go of the steering wheel with your other hand.

sec: Controlling the Vehicle › Hand-Over-Hand Steering · item 4
text: Reach across the arm still holding the wheel, grip the wheel, and pull up.

sec: Controlling the Vehicle › One-Hand Steering · ¶1
text: There are only two situations that may require steering with one hand:

sec: Controlling the Vehicle › One-Hand Steering · item 1
text: When you are turning while backing up to see where you are going behind you. Place your hand at the 12 o’clock position on the steering wheel.

sec: Controlling the Vehicle › One-Hand Steering · item 2
text: When you are operating vehicle controls that require you to remove a hand from the steering wheel.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights · ¶1
text: Your signals, horn, and headlights are important for communicating with other drivers, pedestrians, and bicyclists.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · ¶1
text: Always signal when you turn, change lanes, slow down, or stop.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · ¶2
text: You can signal using your vehicle’s signal lights or using hand-and-arm positions. If your signal lights are not functioning, or bright sunlight makes your signal lights hard to see, use the hand-and-arm signals shown in the image below.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · image
Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · image
Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · image
Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · ¶3
text: Bicyclists may signal a turn with their arm held straight out, pointing in the direction they plan to turn.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · ¶4
text: You should signal:

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · item 1
text: At least 100 feet before you turn.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · item 2
text: Before every lane change.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · item 3
text: At least five seconds before you change lanes on a freeway.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · item 4
text: Before pulling next to the curb or away from the curb.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · item 5
text: Even when you do not see other vehicles around you.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · item 6
text: When you are almost through the intersection if you plan to turn shortly after crossing the intersection.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · ¶5
text: Remember to turn off your signal when you no longer need it.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Horn · ¶1
text: Use your vehicle’s horn to let other drivers know you are there or warn others of a hazard. Use your horn to:

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Horn · item 1
text: Avoid collisions.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Horn · item 2
text: Alert oncoming traffic on narrow mountain roads where you cannot see at least 200 feet ahead.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Headlights · ¶1
text: Your vehicle’s headlights help you see what is in front of you. They also make it easier for other drivers to see your vehicle. Dim your high-beam headlights to low beams within 500 feet of a vehicle coming toward you or within 300 feet of a vehicle you are following. It is illegal to drive using only parking lights. Use your headlights:

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Headlights · item 1
text: When it is too dark to see from 1,000 feet away.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Headlights · item 2
text: Beginning 30 minutes after sunset.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Headlights · item 3
text: Until 30 minutes before sunrise.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Headlights · item 4
text: In adverse weather. If you need to use your windshield wipers due to fog, rain, or snow, you must turn on your low-beam headlights.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Headlights · item 5
text: When conditions (such as clouds, dust, smoke, or fog) prevent you from seeing other vehicles.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Headlights · item 6
text: On mountain roads and tunnels (even on sunny days).

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Headlights · item 7
text: When a road sign states that headlights must be on.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Headlights · item 8
text: To help other drivers see your vehicle, especially when the sun is low on the horizon.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Emergency Flashers · ¶1
text: If you can see a collision or hazard ahead, warn drivers behind you using these methods:

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Emergency Flashers · item 1
text: Turn on your emergency flashers.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Emergency Flashers · item 2
text: Lightly tap your brake pedal three or four times.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Emergency Flashers · item 3
text: Use a hand signal when slowing and stopping.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Emergency Flashers · ¶2
text: If you need to stop because of vehicle trouble:

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Emergency Flashers · item 4
text: Turn on your emergency flashers. If your vehicle does not have emergency flashers, use your turn signals.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Emergency Flashers · item 5
text: If possible, pull off the road away from all traffic.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Emergency Flashers · item 6
text: If you cannot get completely off the road, stop where people can see you and your vehicle from behind.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Emergency Flashers · item 7
text: Do not stop just over a hill or just around a curve. Other drivers may not see your vehicle in time to avoid a collision.

sec: Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Emergency Flashers · item 8
text: Call for emergency roadside assistance and stay in your vehicle until help arrives.

sec: Traffic Lanes · ¶1
text: A traffic lane is a section of road for a single line of traffic.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings · ¶1
text: Lane markings on road surfaces help drivers know which part of the road to use and understand traffic rules.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Single Solid Yellow Line · ¶1
text: A single solid yellow line marks the center of a road with two-way traffic. Do not pass a vehicle in front of you if there is only one lane of traffic going your direction and a solid yellow line on your side of the road.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Double Solid Yellow Lines · ¶1
text: Do not pass over double solid yellow lines. Stay to the right of these lines unless you are:

sec: Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Double Solid Yellow Lines · image
text: Double Solid Yellow Lines. End Divided Road Sign and U-Turn OK Sign
cap: Alt text: “Double Solid Yellow Lines. End Divided Road Sign and U-Turn OK Sign”

sec: Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Double Solid Yellow Lines · item 1
text: In a high-occupancy vehicle (HOV) carpool lane that has a designated entrance on the left.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Double Solid Yellow Lines · item 2
text: Instructed by construction or other signs to drive on the other side of the road because your side is closed or blocked.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Double Solid Yellow Lines · item 3
text: Turning left across a single set of double yellow lines to enter or exit a driveway or private road or make a U-turn.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Double Solid Yellow Lines · ¶2
text: Two sets of solid double yellow lines spaced two or more feet apart are considered a barrier. Do not drive on or over this barrier, make a left turn, or make a U-turn across it, except at designated openings.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Broken Yellow Line · ¶1
text: A broken yellow line indicates you may pass if the broken line is next to your driving lane. Only pass when it is safe.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Single Solid White Line · ¶1
text: A single solid white line marks traffic lanes going in the same direction. This includes one-way streets.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Double Solid White Lines · ¶1
text: Double solid white lines indicate a lane barrier between a regular use and a preferential use lane, such as a carpool (HOV) lane. You may also see double solid white lines in or near freeway on and off ramps. Never change lanes over double solid white lines. Wait until you see a single broken white line.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Broken White Lines · ¶1
text: Broken white lines separate traffic lanes on roads with two or more lanes in the same direction.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Broken White Lines · image
text: End of Lane Markings

sec: Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › End of Lane Markings · ¶1
text: Ending freeway and street lanes are usually marked with large broken lines. If you are driving in a lane marked with broken lines, be prepared to exit the freeway or for the lane to end. Look for a sign that tells you to exit or merge.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Yield Line · ¶1
text: A yield line is a line of solid white triangles that shows approaching vehicles where to yield or stop. The triangles point towards approaching vehicles.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Yield Line · image
Traffic Lanes › Choosing a Lane · ¶1
text: Traffic lanes are often referred to by number. The left (or fast) lane is called the Number 1 Lane. The lane to the right of the Number 1 Lane is called the Number 2 Lane. Then the Number 3 Lane, etc.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Choosing a Lane · image

sec: Traffic Lanes › Choosing a Lane · ¶2
text: Example of numbered traffic lanes

sec: Traffic Lanes › Choosing a Lane · ¶3
text: Here are some tips for choosing a lane:

sec: Traffic Lanes › Choosing a Lane · item 1
text: Use the left lane to pass or turn left.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Choosing a Lane · item 2
text: Use the right lane to enter or exit traffic or when you enter the road from a curb or shoulder.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Changing Lanes · ¶1
text: Before you change lanes:

sec: Traffic Lanes › Changing Lanes · item 1
text: Signal.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Changing Lanes · item 2
text: Check your mirrors.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Changing Lanes · item 3
text: Check traffic behind and beside you.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Changing Lanes · item 4
text: Look over your shoulder in the direction you plan to move to make sure the lane is clear.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Changing Lanes · item 5
text: Check your blind spots for other vehicles, motorcyclists, and bicyclists. Do not let the vehicle drift into another lane.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Changing Lanes · item 6
text: Be sure there is enough space for your vehicle in the next lane. It is not necessary to slow down before a lane change.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Changing Lanes · ¶2
text: Stay in one lane as much as possible. Do not weave in and out of traffic. Last minute lane or direction changes may increase the risk of collisions. Once you start moving through an intersection, keep going. If you start to make a turn, follow through. If you miss a turn, keep driving until you can safely and legally turn around.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Passing Lanes · ¶1
text: On a multilane road, the passing lane (far left lane) is the lane closest to the center divider and is used to pass other vehicles.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Carpool/High-Occupancy Vehicle (HOV) Lanes · ¶1
text: An HOV lane is a special lane reserved for carpools, buses, motorcycles, or low-emission vehicles with decals. To use an HOV lane, one of these must apply:

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Carpool/High-Occupancy Vehicle (HOV) Lanes · image
Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Carpool/High-Occupancy Vehicle (HOV) Lanes · image
Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Carpool/High-Occupancy Vehicle (HOV) Lanes · item 1
text: You have a certain number of people in your vehicle. There will be signs at the on-ramp or along the road to tell you the minimum number of people. Road signs also list the hours when the HOV rules apply.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Carpool/High-Occupancy Vehicle (HOV) Lanes · item 2
text: You are driving a low emission or zero emission vehicle. You must display a special DMV-issued decal.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Carpool/High-Occupancy Vehicle (HOV) Lanes · item 3
text: You are riding a motorcycle (unless otherwise posted).

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Carpool/High-Occupancy Vehicle (HOV) Lanes · ¶2
text: The road surface in a HOV lane is marked with a diamond symbol and the words Carpool Lane. Do not cross over double solid lines to enter or exit an HOV lane. Use designated entrances and exits.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Center Left Turn Lanes · ¶1
text: A center left turn lane is located in the middle of a two-way street. It is marked on both sides by two painted lines. The inner line is broken and the outer line is solid. Use the center left turn lane to prepare for and make a left turn or U-turn. It is not a regular traffic lane or passing lane. You may only drive for 200 feet in the center left turn lane. To turn left from this lane:

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Center Left Turn Lanes · item 1
text: Look for other vehicles coming toward you in the center left turn lane.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Center Left Turn Lanes · item 2
text: Signal.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Center Left Turn Lanes · item 3
text: Look over your shoulder to check your blind spots.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Center Left Turn Lanes · item 4
text: Merge completely into the center left turn lane so you do not block traffic.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Center Left Turn Lanes · item 5
text: Turn when it is safe.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Center Left Turn Lanes · ¶2

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Turnout Areas or Lanes · ¶1
text: Some two-lane roads have special turnout areas or lanes. Merge into these areas or lanes to allow cars behind you to pass.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Turnout Areas or Lanes · image
text: Slower Traffic Use Turnouts
cap: Alt text: “Slower Traffic Use Turnouts”

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Turnout Areas or Lanes · ¶2
text: You must use a turnout area or lane to let other vehicles pass when you are driving slowly on a two-lane road, where passing is unsafe, and there are five or more vehicles following you.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · ¶1
text: Bicycle lanes are for bicyclists only and run alongside vehicle traffic. They are typically marked by a single solid white line and signs. They are sometimes painted bright green to make them easier to see.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · image
text: Bicycle Lane
cap: Alt text: “Bicycle Lane”

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · ¶2
text: Example of shared roadway. Three (3) feet of distance must be maintained between the car and cyclist.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · ¶3
text: It is illegal to drive in a bicycle lane unless you are:

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · item 1
text: Parking (where permitted).

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · item 2
text: Entering or leaving the road.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · item 3
text: Turning (within 200 feet of an intersection).

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · ¶4
text: There are multiple types of bike lanes and markings:

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · item 4
text: Bike lane: Established along streets adjacent to vehicle traffic. Typically marked by a single solid white line that turns into a dash-line near an intersection.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · item 5
text: Buffered bike lane: Uses chevrons or diagonal markings to provide greater separation from traffic and on-street parking.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · item 6
text: Bike route: Uses bike route signs and shared road markings to designate a preferred route for bicyclists on streets shared with vehicle traffic.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · item 7
text: Bicycle boulevard: Prioritizes bicycle travel on streets shared with vehicle traffic.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · item 8
text: Separated bikeway: Is physically separated from motor vehicle traffic and for exclusive use of bicyclists. They are also known as a cycle track or protected bike lanes. The separation may include flexible posts, grade separation, inflexible barriers, or on-street parking.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · item 9
text: Shared roadway bicycle markings: Alert drivers that bicyclists can occupy the lane and help bicyclists maintain a safe lane position in traffic.

sec: Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · ¶5
text: Note Check your blind spots before entering a bike lane. If you drive a motorized bicycle, use caution to avoid other bicyclists. Travel at a reasonable speed and do not endanger the safety of other bicyclists.

sec: Turns › Right Turns · ¶1
text: Example of a right turn.

sec: Turns › Right Turns · ¶2
text: To make a right turn:­

sec: Turns › Right Turns · item 1
text: Drive close to the right edge of the road.

sec: Turns › Right Turns · item 2
text: If a designated right turn lane is available, enter at the opening.

sec: Turns › Right Turns · item 3
text: You can drive in a bike lane within 200 feet from the turn. Check for bicyclists in your blind spots.

sec: Turns › Right Turns · item 4
text: Watch for pedestrians, bicyclists, or motorcyclists between your vehicle and the curb.

sec: Turns › Right Turns · item 5
text: Start signaling about 100 feet before the turn.

sec: Turns › Right Turns · item 6
text: Look over your right shoulder and reduce your speed.

sec: Turns › Right Turns · item 7
text: Stop behind the limit line. A limit line is a wide white line that shows the drivers where to stop before an intersection or crosswalk. If there is no limit line, stop before you enter the crosswalk. If there is no crosswalk, stop before you enter the intersection.

sec: Turns › Right Turns · item 8
text: Look both ways (left-right-left) and turn when it is safe.

sec: Turns › Right Turns · item 9
text: Complete your turn in the right lane. Do not turn wide into another lane.

sec: Turns › Right Turns › Right Turn Against a Red Light · ¶1
path: Right Turn Against a Red Light
text: You may turn right at a red light after a complete stop unless there is a No Turn on Red sign. Follow the same steps listed above for right turns.

sec: Turns › Right Turns › Right Turn Against a Red Arrow · ¶1
path: Right Turn Against a Red Arrow
text: You may not turn right if you are stopped at a red arrow light. Wait until the light changes to green before making your turn.

sec: Turns › Right Turns › Right Turn at a Public Transit Bus Lane · ¶1
path: Right Turn at a Public Transit Bus Lane
text: It is illegal to drive, stop, park, or leave a vehicle in an area designated for public transit buses. Signs will be posted to indicate the lanes are for bus only use. However, you may cross a bus lane to make a right turn.

sec: Turns › Right Turns › Right Turn onto a Road with a Dedicated Lane · ¶1
path: Right Turn onto a Road with a Dedicated Lane
text: A dedicated right turn lane does not merge into another lane and allows you to make a right turn without stopping. You may make your turn even if there is a red light for vehicles going straight through the intersection. If there is a traffic light or sign on the right curb of the right turn lane, you must obey that light or sign. Always yield to pedestrians in a crosswalk when turning.

text: Left Turn

sec: Turns › Left Turns · ¶1
text: Example of a left turn.

sec: Turns › Left Turns · ¶2
text: To turn left:

sec: Turns › Left Turns · item 1
text: Drive close to the center divider or into the left turn lane.

sec: Turns › Left Turns · item 2
text: Enter a designated left turn lane at the opening. Do not cross any solid line.

sec: Turns › Left Turns · item 3
text: Enter a two-way center left turn lane within 200 feet of the turn. Respect the right-of-way of any vehicle, bicyclist, or motorcyclist already in the lane. Always yield to pedestrians.

sec: Turns › Left Turns · item 4
text: Start signaling 100 feet before the turn.

sec: Turns › Left Turns · item 5
text: Look over your left shoulder and reduce your speed.

sec: Turns › Left Turns · item 6
text: Stop behind the limit line. If there is no limit line, stop before you enter the crosswalk. If there is no crosswalk, stop before you enter the intersection.

sec: Turns › Left Turns · item 7
text: Look both ways (left-right-left) and begin your turn when it is safe.

sec: Turns › Left Turns · item 8
text: Proceed into the intersection while turning to complete your turn in the left lane.

sec: Turns › Left Turns · item 9
text: Do not turn the steering wheel too soon and enter the lane of oncoming vehicles.

sec: Turns › Left Turns · item 10
text: Keep your wheels pointed straight ahead until it is safe to start your turn. If your wheels are pointed to the left and a vehicle hits you from behind, you could be pushed into oncoming traffic.

sec: Turns › Left Turns · item 11
text: Accelerate smoothly during and after the turn.

sec: Turns › Left Turns · item 12
text: Allow the steering wheel to straighten in the new lane.

sec: Turns › Left Turns › Left Turn Against a Red Light · ¶1
path: Left Turn Against a Red Light
text: You may turn left against a red light when you are turning from a one-way street onto a one-way street. Make sure there is no sign prohibiting the turn. Yield to other vehicles, pedestrians, or bicyclists who have a green light. Look both ways and turn when it is safe.

sec: Turns › U-TURN · ¶1
text: A U-turn is when you turn your vehicle around to go back in the direction you came. To make a U-turn, signal and use the left turn lane or far-left lane. You may make a U-turn:

sec: Turns › U-TURN · item 1
text: Across a double yellow line.

sec: Turns › U-TURN · item 2
text: In a residential district if no vehicles are approaching you within 200 feet.

sec: Turns › U-TURN · item 3
text: At an intersection on a green traffic light or green arrow, unless a NO U-TURN sign is posted.

sec: Turns › U-TURN · item 4
text: On a divided highway if a center divider opening is provided.

sec: Turns › U-TURN · ¶2
text: Never make a U-turn:

sec: Turns › U-TURN · item 5
text: Where a NO U-TURN sign is posted.

sec: Turns › U-TURN · item 6
text: At or on a railroad crossing.

sec: Turns › U-TURN · item 7
text: On a divided highway by crossing a dividing section, curb, strip of land, or two sets of double yellow lines.

sec: Turns › U-TURN · item 8
text: When you cannot see clearly for 200 feet in each direction.

sec: Turns › U-TURN · item 9
text: On a one-way street.

sec: Turns › U-TURN · item 10
text: In front of a fire station. Never use a fire station driveway to turn around.

sec: Turns › U-TURN · item 11
text: In business districts (the part of a city or town where most offices and businesses are).

sec: Turns › U-TURN · item 12
text: Except at an intersection, or on a divided highway where an opening has been provided.

sec: Turns › Examples of Turns · ¶1
text: The descriptions below refer to the numbers next to the cars in the images. Watch for pedestrians, motorcycles, and bicycles between your vehicle and the curb. When making turns, there may be signs or arrows that indicate you can turn from or end in more than one lane.

sec: Turns › Examples of Turns · item 1
text: Left turn from a two-way street. Start the turn in the left lane closest to the middle of the street. To reduce the risk of collision, end the turn in the left lane closest to the middle of the street going in your vehicle’s direction.

sec: Turns › Examples of Turns · ¶2
text: 2. Right turn. Begin and end the turn in the lane closest to the right edge of the road. Do not swing wide into another lane of traffic.

sec: Turns › Examples of Turns · ¶3
text: 3. Left turn from a two-way street onto a one-way street. Start the turn from the lane closest to the middle of the street (far-left lane). If there are three or more lanes in your direction of travel, you may end your turn in any lane that is open.

sec: Turns › Examples of Turns · ¶4
text: 4. Left turn from a one-way street onto a two-way street. Start the turn from the far-left lane. To reduce the risk of collision, end the turn in the left lane closest to the middle of the street going in your vehicle’s direction.

sec: Turns › Examples of Turns · ¶5
text: 5. Left turn from a one-way street onto a one-way street. Start the turn from the far-left lane. Bicyclists can legally use the left turn lane for their left turns. If there are three or more lanes in your direction of travel, you may end your turn in any lane that is open.

sec: Turns › Examples of Turns · ¶6
text: 6. Right turn from a one-way street onto a one-way street. Start the turn in the far-right lane. If safe, you may end the turn in any lane.

text: 7. Turn at a “T” intersection from a one-way street onto a two-way street. Traffic going straight through the intersection has the right-of-way. You may turn either right or left from the center lane.

sec: Turns › Braking · item 1
text: Remove your foot from the accelerator and allow the vehicle to slow down. Lightly press the brake until you come to a full stop. Give yourself enough space and time to perform this maneuver.

sec: Turns › Braking · item 2
text: When stopping at a limit line, do not cross over the line. If stopping behind a vehicle, leave enough space to see their rear wheels.

sec: Merging And Exiting › Merging · ¶1
text: Highway traffic has the right-of-way. For more information, see Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First in Section 7. When you enter a highway, you will need to:

sec: Merging And Exiting › Merging · item 1
text: Be in the proper lane on the on-ramp.

sec: Merging And Exiting › Merging · item 2
text: Be at or near the speed of traffic.

sec: Merging And Exiting › Merging · item 3
text: Merge into highway traffic when safe to do so. Do not stop unless absolutely necessary.

sec: Merging And Exiting › Merging · item 4
text: Merge into a space large enough for your vehicle to safely join the lane.

sec: Merging And Exiting › Merging · item 5
text: Use your mirrors and turn signals.

sec: Merging And Exiting › Merging · item 6
text: Turn your head quickly to look over your shoulder before changing lanes or merging into traffic.

sec: Merging And Exiting › Merging · item 7
text: Make sure you can stop safely by leaving three seconds of space between you and the vehicle in front of you.

sec: Merging And Exiting › Merging · item 8
text: Make sure you do not cross over any solid lines when merging. If you need to cross several lanes, signal and cross them one at a time. Check your blind spots for vehicles, motorcyclists, bicyclists, and pedestrians each time.

sec: Merging And Exiting › Exiting · ¶1
text: To exit a highway safely:

sec: Merging And Exiting › Exiting · item 1
text: Know your exit and be aware of when it is approaching.

sec: Merging And Exiting › Exiting · item 2
text: If you plan to change lanes, do so one at a time. Signal and look over your shoulder to check your blind spots.

sec: Merging And Exiting › Exiting · item 3
text: When in the proper lane, signal five seconds (approximately 400 feet) before you exit.

sec: Merging And Exiting › Exiting · item 4
text: Make sure you are at a safe speed to exit.

sec: Merging And Exiting › Exiting · item 5
text: Do not cross over any solid lines when exiting.

sec: Merging And Exiting › Crossing or Entering Traffic · ¶1
text: When entering traffic from a full stop, signal and leave a large enough space to get up to the speed of traffic. To merge, enter, or exit traffic, you need a space that is:

sec: Merging And Exiting › Crossing or Entering Traffic · item 1
text: Half a block on city streets, which is about 150 feet.

sec: Merging And Exiting › Crossing or Entering Traffic · item 2
text: A full block on the highway, which is about 300 feet.

sec: Merging And Exiting › Crossing or Entering Traffic · ¶2
text: Even if you have a green light, do not start across the intersection if there are pedestrians or vehicles blocking your pathway.

sec: Merging And Exiting › Crossing or Entering Traffic · ¶3
text: When turning left, do not assume that an oncoming vehicle with its right turn signal on is turning before it reaches you. The driver may have their signal on by mistake or plan to turn just beyond you. Wait for the vehicle to start its turn before beginning the left turn.

sec: Passing · ¶1
text: You must judge whether you have enough space to pass whenever you approach:

sec: Passing · item 1
text: An oncoming vehicle or bicyclist.

sec: Passing · item 2
text: A hill, curve, intersection, or road obstruction. To safely pass, the hill or curve should be at least one-third of a mile ahead.

sec: Passing · ¶2
text: Before you pass, look ahead for road conditions that may cause other vehicles to move into your lane.

sec: Passing · ¶3
text: Do not pass:

sec: Passing · item 3
text: If you are approaching a hill or curve and cannot see if other traffic is approaching. This is very dangerous on one and two lane roads.

sec: Passing · item 4
text: Within 100 feet of an intersection, bridge, tunnel, railroad crossing, or other hazardous area.

sec: Passing · item 5
text: At crossroads and driveways.

sec: Passing · item 6
text: Unless you have enough space to return to your lane.

sec: Passing › How to Pass · ¶1
text: When you are going to pass on an open highway:

sec: Passing › How to Pass · item 1
text: Signal that you plan on passing.

sec: Passing › How to Pass · item 2
text: Look over your shoulder to check your blind spots.

sec: Passing › How to Pass · item 3
text: Drive into the passing lane.

sec: Passing › How to Pass · item 4
text: Speed up to pass the vehicle.

sec: Passing › How to Pass · item 5
text: Signal and return to your original lane.

sec: Passing › How to Pass · ¶2
text: You may pass on the right only when:

sec: Passing › How to Pass · item 6
text: An open highway has two or more lanes going in your direction.

sec: Passing › How to Pass · item 7
text: The driver ahead of you is turning left and you can safely pass on the right. Never pass on the left if the driver is signaling a left turn.

sec: Passing › How to Pass · item 8
text: You are on a one-way street.

sec: Passing › How to Pass · ¶3
text: Never drive off the paved or main-traveled part of the road to pass.

sec: Passing › Being Passed · ¶1
text: If a vehicle is passing you or signals that they plan on passing, allow the vehicle to pass. Maintain your lane position and your speed.

sec: Parking › Parallel Parking · ¶1
text: Parallel parking is when you park in line with the road and other parked vehicles. To parallel park:

sec: Parking › Parallel Parking · ¶2
text: 1. Find a space. Look for a space at least three feet longer than your vehicle. When you find a space, turn on your signal to show that you plan on parking.

sec: Parking › Parallel Parking · ¶3
text: 2. Pull up alongside the vehicle in front of the space. Leave about two feet between your vehicle and the vehicle next to you. Stop once your rear bumper is aligned with the front of your parking space. Keep your signal on.

sec: Parking › Parallel Parking · image
text: Find a parallel parking space
cap: Alt text: “Find a parallel parking space”

sec: Parking › Parallel Parking · ¶4
text: 3. Check your blind spots. Look in your rearview mirror and over your shoulder for approaching vehicles and pedestrians.

sec: Parking › Parallel Parking · ¶5
text: 4. Begin backing up. Turn your steering wheel to back into the space at about a 45-degree angle.

sec: Parking › Parallel Parking · image
text: Parallel Parking: Checking Blind Spots
cap: Alt text: “Parallel Parking: Checking Blind Spots”

sec: Parking › Parallel Parking · ¶6
text: 5. Straighten out. Begin turning the steering wheel away from the curb when your rear wheel is within 18 inches of the curb. You may need to pull forward and backward to straighten out. Your vehicle should now be parallel and within 18 inches of the curb.

sec: Parking › Parallel Parking · image
text: Parallel Parking
cap: Alt text: “Parallel Parking”

sec: Parking › Parallel Parking · ¶7
text: Turn off your vehicle and set the parking brake. Before you exit your vehicle, look carefully for passing vehicles, bicycles, and motorcycles. Exit when safe.

sec: Parking › Straight Line Backing · ¶1
text: To back up in a straight line:

sec: Parking › Straight Line Backing · item 1
text: Traffic check. Observe traffic and check appropriate blind spots.

sec: Parking › Straight Line Backing · item 2
text: Signal . Activate the turn signal before pulling up to the curb. Cancel the turn signal once completed.

sec: Parking › Straight Line Backing · item 3
text: Check your blind spots. Look in your rearview mirror and over your shoulder for approaching vehicles and pedestrians.

sec: Parking › Straight Line Backing · item 4
text: Begin backing up. Back in a straight line for three vehicle lengths while remaining within three feet of the curb. Stay aware of what is behind you when backing up.

sec: Parking › Straight Line Backing · item 5
text: Control. To maintain control of the vehicle, back at a smooth, safe speed and adjust the steering wheel when needed. Practice until you can keep the vehicle straight. Repeat steps 1 and 2 to pull away from the curb.

sec: Parking › Parking on a Hill · image
Parking › Parking on a Hill · ¶1
text: When you park on a hill, your vehicle could roll due to equipment failure. Remember to set the parking brake and leave the vehicle in park, or in gear for manual transmission. To park:

sec: Parking › Parking on a Hill · item 1
text: On a sloping driveway: Turn the wheels so the vehicle will not roll into the street, leave the vehicle in park and set the parking brake.

sec: Parking › Parking on a Hill · item 2
text: Headed downhill: Turn your front wheels into the curb or right toward the side of the road.

sec: Parking › Parking on a Hill · item 3
text: Headed uphill: Turn your front wheels away from the curb (left-towards the center of the road) and let your vehicle roll back a few inches. The wheel should gently touch the curb.

sec: Parking › Parking on a Hill · item 4
text: Headed either uphill or downhill when there is no curb: Turn the wheels to the right so the vehicle will roll away from the center of the road if the brakes fail.

sec: Parking › Parking at Colored Curbs · ¶1
text: Painted colored curbs have special parking rules.

sec: Parking › Parking at Colored Curbs · item 1
text: White : Stop only long enough to pick up or drop off passengers.

sec: Parking › Parking at Colored Curbs · item 2
text: Green : Park for a limited time. The time limit may be posted on signs or painted on the curb.

sec: Parking › Parking at Colored Curbs · item 3
text: Yellow : Load and unload passengers and freight. Do not stop longer than the time posted. If you drive a noncommercial vehicle, you are usually required to stay with your vehicle.

sec: Parking › Parking at Colored Curbs · item 4
text: Red : No stopping, standing, or parking. Buses may stop at a red zone marked for buses only.

sec: Parking › Parking at Colored Curbs · item 5
text: Blue : Parking for a disabled person or someone driving a disabled person with a special placard or special license plate.

sec: Parking › Parking at Colored Curbs · item 6
text: To learn more about disabled parking placards and license plates, visit dmv.ca.gov/disabled-person-parking .

sec: Parking › Illegal Parking · ¶1
text: Never park or leave your vehicle:

sec: Parking › Illegal Parking · item 1
text: Where a NO PARKING sign is posted.

sec: Parking › Illegal Parking · item 2
text: On a marked or unmarked crosswalk.

sec: Parking › Illegal Parking · item 3
text: On a sidewalk, partially blocking a sidewalk, or in front of a driveway.

sec: Parking › Illegal Parking · item 4
text: Within three feet of a sidewalk ramp for disabled persons.

sec: Parking › Illegal Parking · item 5
text: In front of or on a curb that provides wheelchair access to a sidewalk.

sec: Parking › Illegal Parking · item 6
text: In the crosshatched (diagonal lines) area next to a designated disabled parking space.

sec: Parking › Illegal Parking · item 7
text: In a space designated for parking or fueling zero-emission vehicles, unless you are driving a zero-emission vehicle.

sec: Parking › Illegal Parking · item 8
text: In a tunnel or on a bridge, unless permitted by signs.

sec: Parking › Illegal Parking · item 9
text: Within 15 feet of a fire hydrant or fire station driveway.

sec: Parking › Illegal Parking · item 10
text: Within 20 feet of an unmarked or marked crosswalk, or within 15 feet of a crosswalk where a curb extension is present.

sec: Parking › Illegal Parking · item 11
text: Between a safety zone and curb.

sec: Parking › Illegal Parking · item 12
text: Double parked.

sec: Parking › Illegal Parking · item 13
text: On the wrong side of the street or on a freeway, except:

sec: Parking › Illegal Parking · item 14
text: In an emergency.

sec: Parking › Illegal Parking · item 15
text: When a law enforcement officer requires a stop.

sec: Parking › Illegal Parking · item 16
text: Where a stop is specifically permitted.

sec: Parking › Illegal Parking · ¶2
text: If you must stop on a freeway, park completely off the pavement and stay in your vehicle with the doors locked until help arrives. A vehicle that is stopped, parked, or left standing on a freeway for more than four hours may be removed.

sec: Parking › Electric Vehicles · ¶1
text: Local authorities can reserve parking spaces on public streets for electric vehicle charging.

sec: Driving Green · ¶1
text: Maximize your fuel efficiency while helping to lower emissions by following these practices:

sec: Driving Green · item 1
text: Speed up and slow down smoothly. Drive at a steady speed.

sec: Driving Green · item 2
text: Regularly inflate your tires, get oil changes, and check filters.

sec: Driving Green · item 3
text: Get rid of extra weight in your vehicle.

sec: Driving Green · ¶2
text: For more information, visit fueleconomy.gov .

sec: Law Enforcement Stops › During a Law Enforcement Stop · item 1
text: Turn on your right turn signal to acknowledge that you see the officer.

sec: Law Enforcement Stops › During a Law Enforcement Stop · item 2
text: Move completely onto the right shoulder, even if in the carpool/HOV lane. Stop in a well-lit area when possible.

sec: Law Enforcement Stops › During a Law Enforcement Stop · item 3
text: Turn off your radio.

sec: Law Enforcement Stops › During a Law Enforcement Stop · item 4
text: Remain inside your vehicle unless directed to get out by the officer.

sec: Law Enforcement Stops › During a Law Enforcement Stop · item 5
text: Roll down your window after stopping your vehicle and before the officer makes contact with you.

sec: Law Enforcement Stops › During a Law Enforcement Stop · item 6
text: The driver and all passengers should place their hands in clear view before the officer makes contact with them.

sec: Law Enforcement Stops › During a Law Enforcement Stop · ¶1
text: Law enforcement officers must state the reason for a traffic or pedestrian stop before they begin any questioning related to a criminal investigation or traffic violation. An exception is made if an officer reasonably believes withholding the reason is necessary to protect life or property from imminent threat. The reason for the stop must be documented on the traffic citation also known as a traffic ticket issued or law enforcement report completed.

sec: Law Enforcement Stops › Your Rights During the Enforcement Stop · ¶1
path: Your Rights During the Enforcement Stop
text: If an officer asks your permission to do something, you have a right to say no. However, if you say no and the officer says they are going to do it anyway, you do not have a right to interfere with their actions. For example, an officer may request to search part or all of your vehicle. You have a right to decline that request, but the officer may have the legal authority to search your vehicle under certain circumstances. If you do not want the officer to search your vehicle, you should clearly say that you do not give your permission, but you do not have a right to resist or obstruct the officer if they search your vehicle.

sec: Law Enforcement Stops › Your Rights During the Enforcement Stop · ¶2
path: Your Rights During the Enforcement Stop
text: The driver of a stopped vehicle must produce a driver’s license, proof of insurance, and vehicle registration when stopped by law enforcement. If a driver does not produce these documents, officers may conduct a limited search for them. An officer may also request the names or identification of passengers. Passengers can decline that request, but under some circumstances the passengers may be required to identify themselves. If passengers do not want to produce their identification, they should clearly say so. Passengers should not interfere with the officer’s duties in conducting the traffic stop, and if an officer demands identification, passengers should not interfere with the officer’s actions. During a traffic stop, an officer can legally require the driver and all passengers to exit or stay inside the vehicle. If you are told to exit the vehicle or stay inside, you must do so.

sec: Law Enforcement Stops › Your Rights During the Enforcement Stop · ¶3
path: Your Rights During the Enforcement Stop
text: In California, only federal law enforcement officers can ask you about your immigration status. California law prohibits state and local officers from asking drivers or passengers about their immigration status. If a California law enforcement officer asks you about your immigration status, you can decline to answer.

sec: Law Enforcement Stops › Your Rights During the Enforcement Stop · ¶4
path: Your Rights During the Enforcement Stop
text: In general, the First Amendment protects the right of drivers and passengers to record interactions with law enforcement in public spaces. If you are recording, you should immediately make that clear. You do not have a right to interfere with the officer’s lawful duties during the enforcement stop, and you should not reach into concealed areas to retrieve your recording device without the officer’s permission. If your recording is not interfering with the officer’s ability to lawfully do their job, an officer cannot confiscate your recording device, delete the recording, or destroy the device just because you are using it to record. In general, you also have the right to deny a request to unlock a cellular phone or provide a password to it, though under some circumstances, such as if you are on parole, you may have to give permission in response to such requests. Finally, no government employee can retaliate against you just because you recorded something in public.

sec: Law Enforcement Stops › Your Rights During the Enforcement Stop · ¶5
path: Your Rights During the Enforcement Stop
text: Even if you believe your rights were violated, you should not engage in physical resistance or violence against the officer. If an officer does something that you believe violates your rights, you can voice your objection, but you should not physically resist. Everyone has the right to be safe during a traffic stop. Your safety and the officer’s safety could be jeopardized if the situation escalates with physical resistance or violence. All members of the public have a right to file a complaint against any law enforcement agency, and it is against the law for any government employee to retaliate against you for doing so. You can file a complaint with the law enforcement agency that employs the officer. You have a right to be free from discrimination based on your actual or perceived race, sex, color, ethnicity, national origin, age, religion, gender identity or expression, sexual orientation, mental or physical disability, medical condition, or citizenship status. You also have other rights guaranteed by the United States and California Constitutions, as well as California and federal laws. When you file a complaint, the agency that employs the officer must investigate the complaint. Links to contact information for California law enforcement agencies can be found at post.ca.gov/le-agencies .

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Traffic Control · ¶1
text: When at or approaching traffic signals or signs, yield to pedestrians, bicyclists, and other nearby vehicles that may have the right-of-way. See Right of Way Rules: Who Goes First , in this section.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Traffic Control › Traffic Signals › Solid Red Light · ¶1
text: A red traffic signal light means STOP. You can turn right at a red light, if:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Traffic Control › Traffic Signals › Solid Red Light · item 1
text: There is not a NO TURN ON RED sign posted.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Traffic Control › Traffic Signals › Solid Red Light · item 2
text: You stop at the stop or limit line, yield for pedestrians, and turn when it is safe.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Traffic Control › Traffic Signals › Red Arrow · ¶1
text: A red arrow means STOP. Do not turn at a red arrow. Remain stopped until a green traffic signal light or green arrow appears.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Traffic Control › Traffic Signals › Flashing Red Light · ¶1

sec: Traffic Control › Traffic Signals › Solid Yellow Light · ¶1
text: A yellow traffic signal light means CAUTION. The light is about to turn red. When you see a yellow traffic signal light, stop, if you can do so safely. If you cannot stop safely, cautiously cross the intersection.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Traffic Control › Traffic Signals › Yellow Arrow · ¶1
text: A yellow arrow means the protected turning time is ending. The signal will change soon. If you cannot stop safely or you are already in the intersection, cautiously complete your turn. Pay attention to the next signal. It could be a:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Traffic Control › Traffic Signals › Yellow Arrow · item 1
text: Green or red traffic signal light.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Traffic Control › Traffic Signals › Yellow Arrow · item 2
text: Red Arrow.

sec: Traffic Control › Traffic Signals › Flashing Yellow Light · ¶1
text: A flashing yellow traffic signal light is a warning to PROCEED WITH CAUTION. Slow down and be alert. You do not need to stop.

sec: Traffic Control › Traffic Signals › Flashing Yellow Arrow · ¶1
text: You can turn, but your turn is not protected from other traffic. Proceed to turn left after yielding to oncoming traffic and proceed with caution.

sec: Traffic Control › Traffic Signals › Solid Green Light · ¶1
text: A green traffic signal light means GO. You should still stop for any vehicle, bicyclist, or pedestrian in the intersection. Only proceed if you have enough space without creating a danger to any oncoming vehicle, bicyclist, or pedestrian. Do not enter the intersection if you cannot get completely across before the traffic signal light turns red.

sec: Traffic Control › Traffic Signals › Green Arrow · ¶1
text: A green arrow means GO in the direction the arrow is pointing. The green arrow allows you to make a protected turn. Oncoming vehicles are stopped by a red traffic signal light.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Traffic Control › Traffic Signals › Traffic Light Not Working · ¶1
text: When a traffic light is not working, stop as if the intersection is controlled by STOP signs in all directions. Then proceed cautiously when it is safe to do so.

text: These are crisscross and diagonal crosswalks that allow pedestrians to cross the intersection in any direction at the same time. Cross only when the walk signal allows it.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Traffic Control › Pedestrian Signals and Signs › Sounds · ¶1
text: Sounds such as beeping, chirping, or verbal messages help blind or visually impaired pedestrians cross the street.

sec: Traffic Control › Pedestrian Signals and Signs › No Pedestrian Signals · ¶1
text: If there are no pedestrian signals, obey the vehicle traffic signals.

text: Obey all warning signs regardless of their shape or color.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? · ¶1
text: Right-of-way rules help you understand who goes first when vehicles, pedestrians, and bicyclists meet on the road. The vehicle that arrives to the intersection first has the right-of-way. Other vehicles, bicyclists, and pedestrians must wait for the person who has the right-of-way. Never assume that other drivers will give you the right-of-way. Give up your right-of-way when it will help prevent collisions.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Intersections · ¶1
text: An intersection is any place where one road meets another road. Controlled intersections have signs or traffic signal lights. Uncontrolled and blind intersections do not. Before entering an intersection, look left, right, and ahead to check for vehicles, bicyclists, and pedestrians. Be prepared to slow down and stop if necessary. Pedestrians always have the right-of-way. Here are some right-of-way rules at intersections:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Intersections · item 1
text: Without STOP or YIELD signs: The vehicle that arrives to the intersection first has the right-of-way. However, if a vehicle, pedestrian, or bicyclist gets to the intersection at the same time as you, give the right-of-way to the vehicle, pedestrian, or bicyclist on your right. If you approach a stop sign and there is a stop sign on all four corners, stop first and proceed as above.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Intersections · item 2
text: T intersections without STOP or YIELD signs: Vehicles, bicyclists, and pedestrians on the through road (continuing to go straight) have the right-of-way.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Intersections · item 3
text: Turning left: Check for pedestrians. Give the right-of-way to any pedestrian or approaching vehicle that is close enough to be dangerous.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Intersections · item 4
text: Turning right: Always check for pedestrians crossing the street, and motorcycles and bicycles riding next to you.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Intersections · item 5
text: Green traffic signal light: Proceed with caution. Pedestrians have the right-of-way.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Intersections · item 6
text: Entering traffic: When entering traffic, you must proceed with caution and yield to the traffic already occupying the lanes. It is against the law to stop or block an intersection where there is not enough space to completely cross before the traffic signal light turns red.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · ¶1
text: In a roundabout, traffic travels in one direction around a central island.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · ¶2
text: How to use a roundabout:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · item 1
text: Slow down as you approach.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · item 2
text: Yield to all traffic already in the roundabout.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · item 3
text: Enter heading to the right when there is a big enough gap in traffic to merge safely.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · item 4
text: Watch for signs and lane markings that guide you.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · item 5
text: Travel in a counter-clockwise direction. Do not stop or pass.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · item 6
text: Signal when you change lanes or exit.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · item 7
text: If you miss your exit, continue around until you return to your exit.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · ¶3
text: If the roundabout has multiple lanes, choose your entry or exit lane based on your destination. This is shown in the image below. To:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · ¶1
text: These are considered pedestrians or vulnerable road users:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · item 1
text: A person walking.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · item 2
text: A person traveling on something other than a vehicle or bicycle. This includes roller skates, a skateboard, etc.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · item 3
text: A person with a disability using a tricycle, quadricycle, or wheelchair for transportation.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · image
text: Tricycle, Quadricycle, Standard Wheelchair, and Electric Wheelchair next to each other.
cap: Alt text: “Tricycle, Quadricycle, Standard Wheelchair, and Electric Wheelchair next to each other.”

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · ¶2
text: From left to right: Tricycle, Quadricycle, Standard Wheelchair, Electric Wheelchair.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · ¶3
text: Although pedestrians have the right-of-way, they also must follow the rules of the road.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · ¶4
text: When there is a pedestrian crossing a roadway with or without a crosswalk, you must use caution, reduce your speed, or stop to allow the pedestrian to safely finish crossing.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · ¶5
text: Other things to keep in mind:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · item 4
text: Do not pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk. You may not be able to see a pedestrian crossing the street.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · item 5
text: If a pedestrian makes eye contact with you, they are ready to cross the street. Yield to the pedestrian.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · item 6
text: Always allow pedestrians enough time to safely cross a street as some groups such as seniors, people with small children, and people with disabilities may require extra time.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians › Crosswalks · ¶1
text: A crosswalk is the part of the road set aside for pedestrians to safely cross the road. They are often marked with white lines. School crossings may have yellow crosswalk lines. Not all crosswalks are marked.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians › Crosswalks · ¶2
text: Pedestrians have the right-of-way in marked or unmarked crosswalks. If there is a limit line before the crosswalk, stop at the limit line and allow pedestrians to cross the street.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians › Crosswalks · ¶3
text: Some crosswalks have flashing lights. Whether or not the lights are flashing, look for pedestrians and be prepared to stop.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians › Pedestrians who are Blind · ¶1
text: Pedestrians using guide dogs or white canes have the right-of-way at all times. These pedestrians are partially or totally blind. Be careful when you are turning or backing up. This is particularly important if you are driving a hybrid or electric vehicle because blind pedestrians rely on sound to know there is a vehicle nearby.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians › Pedestrians who are Blind · item 1
text: Do not stop in the middle of a crosswalk. This could force a blind pedestrian to walk into traffic outside of the crosswalk.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians › Pedestrians who are Blind · item 2
text: Do not honk your horn at a blind person.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians › Pedestrians who are Blind · item 3
text: When a blind person pulls in their cane and steps away from the intersection, this gesture usually means you may go.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road
sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Mountain Roads · ¶1
text: If two vehicles meet on a steep narrow road and neither vehicle can pass, the vehicle facing uphill has the right-of-way. The vehicle facing downhill has more control when backing up the hill. The vehicle facing downhill should back up until the vehicle going uphill can pass.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road · ¶1
text: Drivers need to share the road with other vehicles, pedestrians, bicyclists, road workers, and large vehicles.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Blind Spots (the No Zone) · ¶1
text: Large vehicle and truck drivers have a better view in front of them and bigger mirrors. But they also have large blind spots, also called No Zones. In these areas, your vehicle can disappear from a large vehicle or truck driver’s view. If you cannot see the truck’s side mirrors, the truck driver cannot see you.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Blind Spots (the No Zone) · image

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Blind Spots (the No Zone) · ¶2
text: The shaded areas in this image are the truck driver’s blind spots.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Braking · ¶1
text: Large vehicles and commercial trucks take longer to stop than passenger vehicles traveling at the same speed. When traveling, they create extra space in front of their vehicle to use if they need to stop suddenly. The average passenger vehicle traveling at 55 mph can stop within 300 feet. A large vehicle traveling at the same speed can take up to 400 feet to stop. The heavier the vehicle and the faster it is moving, the longer it takes to safely stop, so a loaded truck will take longer to stop than an empty truck. Do not move in front of a large vehicle and suddenly slow down or stop. The large vehicle will not be able to stop fast enough to avoid crashing into you.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Turning · ¶1
text: When a vehicle turns, the rear wheels follow a shorter path than the front wheels. The longer the vehicle, the greater the difference in the length of the turning path. This is why large vehicles and truck drivers must often swing wide to complete a turn. When you follow a large vehicle, look at its turn signals before you start to pass. It may appear to be turning one direction but instead is swinging wide in the opposite direction in order to turn.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Maneuvering · ¶1
text: Large vehicles and trucks are not as easy to maneuver as passenger vehicles. On a divided highway with four or more traffic lanes in one direction, they may be driven in the two lanes farthest to the right. When driving near large vehicles and trucks, do not:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Maneuvering · item 1
text: Change lanes directly in front of them to reach an exit or turn.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Maneuvering · item 2
text: Drive next to them longer than you need to. Always pass a large vehicle on the left side. After you pass the large vehicle or truck, move ahead of it. Driving alongside a large vehicle makes it hard for the driver to avoid dangers in the road.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Maneuvering · item 3
text: Follow too closely. Tailgating decreases a vehicle’s safety distance.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Maneuvering · item 4
text: Underestimate their size and speed as they often appear to be traveling slower.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · ¶1
text: Safety zones are spaces set aside for pedestrians waiting for buses, streetcars, and trolleys. Safety zones are marked by raised buttons or markers on a road. Do not drive through a safety zone under any condition.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · ¶2
text: When a bus, streetcar, or trolley is stopped at a safety zone or traffic light, you may pass at no more than 10 mph.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · image
text: Trolley next to demarked safe zone.
cap: Alt text: “Trolley next to demarked safe zone.”

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · ¶3
text: Safe Zones are marked by dotted white lines.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · ¶4
text: Do not overtake and pass a light rail vehicle or streetcar on the left side, whether it is moving or standing, unless:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · item 1
text: When the tracks are so close to the right side that the passenger vehicle cannot pass on the right.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · item 2
text: You are on a one-way street.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · item 3
text: A traffic officer directs you to pass on the left.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Light Rail Vehicles · ¶1
text: On public roads, light rail vehicles have the same rights and responsibilities as other vehicles. To safely share the road with light rail vehicles:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Light Rail Vehicles · item 1
text: Be aware of where they operate. Buildings, trees, and other items can cause blind spots for the operator.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Light Rail Vehicles · item 2
text: Never turn in front of an approaching light rail vehicle.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Light Rail Vehicles · item 3
text: Maintain a safe distance.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Light Rail Vehicles · item 4
text: Check for approaching light rail vehicles before you turn across the tracks. Complete your turn only when the traffic light indicates you may proceed. Be aware they can interrupt traffic lights.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Light Rail Vehicles · image
text: Light rail travelling down street. One car drives parallel to the train, while another car turns directly into the train's path.
cap: Alt text: “Light rail travelling down street. One car drives parallel to the train, while another car turns directly into the train's path.”

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Light Rail Vehicles · ¶2
text: Do not turn in front of light rail vehicles.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Motorcycles · ¶1
text: Motorcyclists have the same rights and responsibilities as other vehicle drivers. To safely share the road with motorcyclists:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Motorcycles · item 1
text: Check for motorcycles and use your mirrors when you change lanes or enter a road. Motorcycles are smaller in size and harder to see so they easily disappear in vehicle blind spots.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Motorcycles · item 2
text: Allow a safe three-second following distance. This space will help you avoid hitting a motorcyclist if they brake suddenly or fall.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Motorcycles · item 3
text: Whenever possible, give a motorcycle the full lane. It is legal to share lanes with motorcycles, this is known as lane splitting.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Motorcycles · item 4
text: Never try to pass a motorcycle in the same lane as you.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Motorcycles · item 5
text: Check for motorcyclists before you open your door next to traffic.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Motorcycles · item 6
text: When possible, move to one side of your lane to give motorcyclists more room to pass.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Motorcycles · ¶2
text: Road conditions can cause motorcyclists to suddenly change speed or direction.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Emergency Vehicles · ¶1
text: Give the right-of-way to any law enforcement vehicle, fire engine, ambulance, or other emergency vehicle using a siren and red lights. Failure to pull over may result in a ticket. Drive to the right edge of the road and stop until the emergency vehicle(s) have passed.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Emergency Vehicles · image
text: Car pulling over to let fire truck pass.
cap: Alt text: “Car pulling over to let fire truck pass.”

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Emergency Vehicles · ¶2
text: Yield to emergency vehicles.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Emergency Vehicles · ¶3
text: When approaching a stationary emergency vehicle with flashing emergency signal lights (hazard lights), move over and slow down.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Emergency Vehicles · ¶4
text: If you are in an intersection when you see an emergency vehicle, continue through the intersection. Drive to the right as soon as it is safe and stop.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Emergency Vehicles · ¶5
text: Obey any direction, order, or signal given by a law enforcement officer, or firefighter. Follow their orders even if they conflict with existing signs, signals, or laws.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Emergency Vehicles · ¶6
text: It is against the law to follow within 300 feet of any fire engine, law enforcement vehicle, ambulance, or other emergency vehicle when their siren or flashing lights are on.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Emergency Vehicles · ¶7
text: You can be arrested if you drive to the scene of a fire, collision, or other disaster. When you do this, you are getting in the way of firefighters, ambulance crews, or other rescue and emergency personnel.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Slow-moving Vehicles · ¶1
text: They can take longer to get up to speed when entering traffic. Large trucks, bicycles, and some cars lose speed on long or steep hills. Some slow-moving vehicles have an orange and red triangle on their back, such as road maintenance vehicles, which usually travel at 25 mph or less.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)

text: Bulldozer with orange-red "slow vehicle" triangle.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Slow-moving Vehicles · ¶3
text: Other types of slow-moving motorized vehicles that may operate on public roads include:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Slow-moving Vehicles · item 1
text: Scooters

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Slow-moving Vehicles · item 2
text: Neighborhood electric vehicles

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Slow-moving Vehicles · item 3
text: Golf carts

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Slow-moving Vehicles · ¶4
text: Adjust your speed to share the road with these vehicles.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Neighborhood Electric Vehicles (NEV) and Low-speed Vehicles (LSV) · ¶1
path: Neighborhood Electric Vehicles (NEV) and Low-speed Vehicles (LSV)
text: Watch for slow-moving vehicles when you see these signs or markings:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Neighborhood Electric Vehicles (NEV) and Low-speed Vehicles (LSV) · item 2
