text: NEV ROUTE

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Neighborhood Electric Vehicles (NEV) and Low-speed Vehicles (LSV) · ¶2
path: Neighborhood Electric Vehicles (NEV) and Low-speed Vehicles (LSV)
text: NEVs and LSVs reach a maximum speed of 25 mph. They are restricted from roads where the speed limit is greater than 35 mph.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Animal-drawn Vehicles · ¶1
text: Horse-drawn vehicles and people riding horses or other animals are allowed to share the road with motor vehicles. It is against the law to intentionally scare horses or livestock.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Near Animals · ¶1
text: If you see a sign with a picture of an animal, watch for animals on or near the road. If you see animals or livestock near the road, slow down or stop and proceed when it is safe. Be sure to follow directions from the person in charge of the animals.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles · ¶1
text: Bicyclists have the same rights and responsibilities as other drivers.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles · ¶2
text: Bicyclists may:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles · item 1
text: Legally ride on certain sections of freeways where there is no alternate route and bicycling is not forbidden by law.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles · item 2
text: Move left to avoid hazards. These may include parked or moving vehicles, bicycles, animals, or trash.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles · item 3
text: Choose to ride near the left curb or edge of a one-way street.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles · item 4
text: Choose to use crosswalks by stopping and crossing as a pedestrian.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · ¶1
text: As a bicyclist, you must:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 1
text: Obey all traffic signs, signal lights, and basic right-of-way rules.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 2
text: Ride in the same direction as traffic.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 3
text: Always look over your shoulder to make sure the lane is clear before turning or changing lanes.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 4
text: Yield to pedestrians.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 5
text: Wear a helmet (if under 18 years old).

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 6
text: Stay visible (for example, never weave between parked vehicles).

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 7
text: Ride as near to the right curb or edge of the roadway as possible.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 8
text: Not ride on the sidewalk (unless allowed by the city).

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 9
text: Make left and right turns in the same way drivers do, using hand signals and turn lanes.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 10
text: Use a bike lane, whenever possible, or use a through traffic lane.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 11
text: Have fully functional brakes.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · ¶3
text: Intersection with special lanes for bicyclists.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling at Night · ¶1
text: When it is dark out, bicyclists should avoid wearing dark clothing. Your bicycle must have the following equipment:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling at Night · item 1
text: A front lamp with a white light visible from 300 feet.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling at Night · item 2
text: A built-in rear red reflector, solid red light, or flashing red light. This must be visible from 500 feet.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling at Night · item 3
text: A white or yellow reflector on each pedal, the bicyclist’s shoes, or their ankles. These must be visible from 200 feet.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling at Night · item 4
text: A white or yellow reflector on the front wheel, a white or red reflector on the rear wheel, or reflectorized tires.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · ¶1
text: Bicyclists traveling slower than the flow of traffic must ride as close as possible to the right curb or edge of the road, unless :

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · item 1
text: Passing a vehicle or another bicycle in the same direction.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · item 2
text: Preparing to make a left turn.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · item 3
text: Avoiding a hazard or road condition.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · item 4
text: A lane is too narrow for a bicycle and a vehicle to safely travel side-by-side in the lane.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · item 5
text: Approaching a right turn.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · item 6
text: On a one-way road with two or more lanes. In this case, a bicyclist may ride near the left curb or edge of the road.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · ¶2
text: Drivers should follow at a safe distance. When it is safe, the bicyclist should move to a position that allows vehicles to pass.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · ¶1
text: To safely pass a bicyclist that is in the travel lane, you may need to change to another lane. In this case, pass safely, then return to your original lane. Leave space between your vehicle and the bicyclist.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · image
text: Car passing a cyclist. The car leaves enough space between itself and the bicyclist as it passes.
cap: Alt text: “Car passing a cyclist. The car leaves enough space between itself and the bicyclist as it passes.”

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · ¶2
text: Right

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · image
text: Car attempting to pass a cyclist without leaving any room. The car hits the cyclist.
cap: Alt text: “Car attempting to pass a cyclist without leaving any room. The car hits the cyclist.”

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · ¶3
text: Wrong

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · ¶4
text: When you cannot change lanes to pass a bicyclist, allow at least three feet between your vehicle and the bicyclist. If you cannot give three feet of space, do not pass the cyclist until three feet of clearance can be given. This will help you avoid putting the bicyclist in danger. Remember to:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · item 1
text: Give bicyclists enough space so they are not forced into parked vehicles or open vehicle doors.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · item 2
text: Only merge toward the curb or into the bike lane when it is safe.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · item 3
text: Merge safely behind a bicyclist when preparing to make a turn.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · item 4
text: Enter a bike lane no more than 200 feet before starting a turn.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · item 5
text: Check for bicyclists when changing lanes or entering traffic. They may be hidden in a vehicle’s blind spots.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · item 6
text: Be careful when approaching or passing a bicyclist on a two-lane road.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones · ¶1
text: You will see warning signs and message boards when there are workers, slow-moving equipment, and closed lanes ahead.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones · ¶2
text: Go through the work zone carefully by:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones · item 1
text: Slowing down.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones · item 2
text: Allowing extra space between vehicles.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones · item 3
text: Expecting sudden slowing or stopping.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones · item 4
text: Watching for drivers changing lanes.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones · item 5
text: Avoiding distractions.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones · ¶3
text: Cones, drums, or other barriers will guide you through the work zone. Prepare to slow down or stop for highway equipment. Merge as soon as it is safe without crossing the cones or drums. Watch for bicycles if lanes are narrow or the shoulder is closed. Obey special signs or instructions from workers such as flaggers.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones › Fines and Double Fine Zones · ¶1
text: Fines for traffic violations in a work zone can be $1,000 or more. Anyone convicted of assaulting a highway worker faces fines of up to $2,000 and imprisonment for up to one year.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones › Fines and Double Fine Zones · ¶2
text: Certain roads are chosen as Safety Enhanced-Double Fine Zones. This is due to increased collision-related injuries and fatalities. Fines are doubled in these zones.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones › Fines and Double Fine Zones · ¶3
text: Fines are also doubled in highway construction or maintenance zones when workers are present.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones › Move Over and Slow Down · ¶1
text: Drivers must move over and slow down for emergency and road work vehicles. These include:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones › Move Over and Slow Down · item 1
text: Stationary emergency vehicles or tow trucks displaying flashing amber warning lights.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones › Move Over and Slow Down · item 2
text: Stopped road work vehicles displaying emergency flashing or amber warning lights.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Vehicles with Hazardous Loads · ¶1
text: A diamond-shaped sign on a truck means that the truck’s load may be dangerous (gas, explosives, etc.). Vehicles with these signs must stop before crossing railroad tracks.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Vehicles with Hazardous Loads · image
text: Hazard symbols for "Flammable," "Radioactive," "Explosives," and "Poison."
cap: Alt text: “Hazard symbols for "Flammable," "Radioactive," "Explosives," and "Poison."”

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Vehicles with Hazardous Loads · ¶2
text: Examples of hazardous load placards.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Heavy Traffic or Bad Weather · ¶1
text: You must drive slower when there is heavy traffic or bad weather. At the same time, you should not block normal and reasonable traffic flow by driving too slowly. If you drive faster or slower than the speed limit, you may be cited. When another driver is close behind you and wishes to drive faster, move to the right. If you choose to drive slower than other traffic, drive in the right lane. Refer to Choosing a Lane in Section 6 for more information.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Towing · ¶1
text: You must drive in the far-right lane or a lane marked for slower vehicles when you:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Towing · item 1
text: Tow a vehicle or trailer.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Towing · item 2
text: Drive a truck with three or more axles.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Towing · ¶2
text: If no lanes are marked and there are four or more lanes in your direction, you may only drive in the two lanes closest to the right edge of the road.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Around Children · image
text: School bus with red lights flashing and a crossing guard next to it. Students are near the bus. Cars are stopped around the bus.
cap: Alt text: “School bus with red lights flashing and a crossing guard next to it. Students are near the bus. Cars are stopped around the bus.”

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Around Children · ¶1
text: All vehicles must stop for school buses.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Around Children · ¶2
text: The speed limit is 25 mph within 500 feet of a school while children are outside or crossing the street. Some school zones may have speed limits as low as 15 mph. When near schools, look for:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Around Children · item 1
text: Bicyclists and pedestrians.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Around Children · item 2
text: School safety patrols or crossing guards. Be sure to obey their directions at all times.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Around Children · item 3
text: Stopped school buses and children crossing the street.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Around Children · item 4
text: Some school buses flash yellow lights when preparing to stop to let children off the bus. The yellow flashing lights warn you to slow down and prepare to stop.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Around Children · item 5
text: When the bus flashes red lights (located at the top, front, and back of the bus), you must stop from either direction until the children are safely across the street and the lights stop flashing. Remain stopped while the red lights are flashing. If you fail to stop, you may be fined up to $1,000 and your driving privilege could be suspended for one year.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Around Children · item 6
text: If the school bus is on the other side of a divided or multilane highway (two or more lanes in each direction), you do not need to stop.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Blind Intersections · ¶1
text: An intersection is considered blind if it has no stop signs at any corner.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Blind Intersections · ¶2
text: If your view is blocked, move slowly forward until you can see. The speed limit for a blind intersection is 15 mph.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Alleys · ¶1
text: An alley is any road no wider than 25 feet that is used to access the rear or side entrances of buildings or properties. You may drive on or cross a sidewalk to enter or exit a driveway or alley. The speed limit in an alley is 15 mph.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks · ¶1
path: Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks
text: The speed limit is 15 mph within 100 feet of a railroad crossing and you cannot see the tracks for 400 feet in both directions. You may drive faster than 15 mph if the crossing is controlled by gates, a warning signal, or a flagman. At railroad or train crossings:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks · item 1
path: Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks
text: Flashing red warning lights indicate you must stop and wait. Do not proceed over the railroad tracks until the red lights stop flashing, even if the gate rises.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks · item 2
path: Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks
text: When the crossing devices or a person warns you a train is coming, stop at least 15 feet from the nearest track.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks · item 3
path: Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks
text: Do not go under lowering gates or around lowered gates. If the gates are lowered and you do not see a train approaching, call the posted railroad emergency toll-free number or 911.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks · item 4
path: Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks
text: Stop, look, and listen. If you see a train coming or hear a horn or bell, do not cross. Many crossings have multiple tracks. Look in both directions and only cross when it is safe.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks · item 5
path: Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks
text: Expect a train on any track, at any time, traveling in either direction.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks · item 6
path: Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks
text: Never stop on the railroad tracks. Wait and do not begin proceeding if you do not have enough room to completely cross the tracks. If you are on the tracks, you risk injury or death.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks · item 7
path: Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks
text: Watch for vehicles that must stop before they cross train tracks. These vehicles include buses, school buses, and vehicles marked with a hazardous materials placard.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Business or Residential Districts · ¶1
text: The speed limit is 25 mph, unless otherwise posted.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information · ¶1
text: You must:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information · item 1
text: Not smoke when a minor is in the vehicle. You can be fined.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information · item 2
text: Not dump or abandon animals on a highway. This crime is punishable by a fine of up to $1,000, six months in jail, or both.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information · item 3
text: Not drive a vehicle so overloaded that you cannot control it, see ahead, or see to the sides of your vehicle.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information · item 4
text: Not drive a vehicle with an unsecured load that is a safety hazard.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information · item 5
text: Not carry anything in or on a passenger vehicle which extends beyond the fenders on the left side or more than 6-inches beyond the fenders on the right side.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information · item 6
text: Cargo that extends more than 4 feet from the back-rear bumper of the vehicle must display a 12-inch red or fluorescent orange square flag.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information · item 7
text: At night, this cargo must be marked with two red lights.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information · item 8
text: Not allow a person to ride in the back of a pickup or other truck unless the vehicle has secure seats and seat (safety) belts.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information · item 9
text: Not transport animals in the back of a pickup or other truck unless the animal is properly secured. This prevents the animal from falling, jumping, or being thrown from the vehicle.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information · item 10
text: Not drive a vehicle equipped with a video monitor visible to the driver, unless it only displays vehicle information, navigation system, media player, or radio.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information · item 11
text: Not throw a cigarette, cigar, or other flaming or glowing substance from your vehicle.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information · item 12
text: Not put signs or other objects on the front windshield or side rear windows that block your view. Do not hang objects on the mirror. Objects may only be affixed in these locations:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information · item 13
text: A 7-inch square on the lower corner of the passenger’s side windshield or the lower corner of the rear window.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information · item 14
text: A 5-inch square on the lower corner of the driver’s side window.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information · item 15
text: A 5-inch square located in the center uppermost portion of your windshield for an electronic toll payment device.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information · item 16
text: On the side windows behind the driver.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information · item 17
text: Not interfere with a funeral procession. A funeral procession is led by a traffic officer and has the right-of-way. All vehicles taking part in the procession have windshield markers to identify them and have their headlights on. You can be ticketed if you interrupt a funeral procession.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information · item 18
text: Not operate a vehicle with an illegible license plate.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information · item 19
text: Not alter a license plate in any way.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Evading Law Enforcement · ¶1
text: It is a misdemeanor to use a motor vehicle to flee or attempt to evade law enforcement performing their duties. This is punishable by imprisonment in a county jail for one year or less.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Evading Law Enforcement · ¶2
text: A person convicted of causing serious bodily injury during a law enforcement pursuit is subject to imprisonment in a state prison for up to seven years, or a county jail for one year or less.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Evading Law Enforcement · ¶3
text: A person convicted of manslaughter resulting from evading law enforcement during a pursuit is subject to imprisonment in a state prison for a minimum of 4 to 10 years.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Evading Law Enforcement · ¶4
text: If an unlicensed person is caught driving your vehicle, it may be impounded for 30 days.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Speed Contests and Reckless Driving · ¶1
text: A person convicted of reckless driving or engaging in a speed contest that causes injury to another person is subject to imprisonment, a fine, or both.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Points on Your Driver’s Record · ¶1
text: DMV monitors your driver’s record. If you are stopped by a law enforcement officer and cited (ticketed) for a traffic violation, you sign the ticket as a promise to appear in traffic court. As an adult or minor, if you get a traffic ticket and fail to appear (FTA) in court, DMV may suspend your driving privilege until you appear. If you do not keep your promise to appear in court, the FTA goes on your driver’s record.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Points on Your Driver’s Record · ¶2
text: Each time you are convicted of a moving traffic violation, the court notifies DMV. The conviction is placed on your driver’s record. Convictions reported by other states and juvenile court are also added to your driver’s record. Traffic convictions and collisions stay on your record for 36 months or longer, depending on the type of conviction. As an adult, your license may be suspended if your driver’s record shows one of the following point totals:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Points on Your Driver’s Record · item 1
text: 4 points in 12 months.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Points on Your Driver’s Record · item 2
text: 6 points in 24 months.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Points on Your Driver’s Record · item 3
text: 8 points in 36 months.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Traffic Violator School · ¶1
text: If you are given a one-point traffic violation, the judge may offer you the choice to attend a traffic violator school to have the citation not reported to your insurance company but remain on your driving record. You can do this once in any 18-month period. The school will report your course completion to the court. You will also get a completion receipt.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Traffic Violator School · ¶2
text: If you are a commercial driver cited in a noncommercial vehicle, see the California Commercial Driver’s Handbook .

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Suspension or Revocation · ¶1
text: If you have too many points on your driver’s record, you will be considered a negligent driver. DMV will place you on probation, suspend, or revoke your driving privilege. When this happens, you have the right to a hearing. DMV will notify you in writing of any action taken against your driving privilege and inform you of your legal rights, including your right to a hearing.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Suspension or Revocation · ¶2
text: DMV will revoke your driving privilege if you are convicted of a hit-and-run or reckless driving that resulted in injury. Courts also have the authority to suspend a person’s driving privilege.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Suspension or Revocation · ¶3
text: At the end of your suspension or revocation, you may apply for a replacement driver’s license. You must show proof of financial responsibility (such as SR 22/SR 1P).

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Maintaining Your Minor’s (Provisional) Driver’s License · ¶1
text: If you get into collisions or commit traffic violations within the first 12 months of obtaining your minor’s driver’s license, DMV may restrict or suspend your driving privilege. You cannot drive if your driving privilege is suspended or revoked.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Maintaining Your Minor’s (Provisional) Driver’s License · ¶2
text: As a minor, DMV may take action against your license if you have:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Maintaining Your Minor’s (Provisional) Driver’s License · item 1
text: One at fault collision or traffic violation conviction: An at fault collision means you were found responsible.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Maintaining Your Minor’s (Provisional) Driver’s License · item 2
text: Two at fault collisions, two traffic violation convictions, or one of each: You cannot drive for 30 days unless a licensed adult, at least 25 years old, rides with you.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Maintaining Your Minor’s (Provisional) Driver’s License · item 3
text: Three at fault collisions, three traffic violation convictions, or a combination: Your driving privilege will be suspended for six months. You will be on probation for one year.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Maintaining Your Minor’s (Provisional) Driver’s License · item 4
text: If you have more at fault collisions or traffic violation convictions while on probation, your license will be suspended again.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Maintaining Your Minor’s (Provisional) Driver’s License · item 5
text: A conviction of using alcohol or a controlled substance, or both and are 15-20 years old: The court will order DMV to suspend your driving privilege for one year or delay your eligibility to apply for a driver’s license.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Maintaining Your Minor’s (Provisional) Driver’s License · ¶3
text: Note Turning 18 years old does not erase or end existing restrictions, suspensions, or probation sentences.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Administrative Hearing · ¶1
text: Administrative hearings are conducted by DMV. If you received notification that a proposed action is being taken against your driving privilege, you must request a hearing within 10 days of being served or 14 days from the date the notice is mailed. If you do not make a timely request, your right to a hearing will be lost.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Administrative Hearing · ¶2
text: This hearing provides you with an opportunity to be heard before an action is taken against your driving privilege. You may also have to appear in court for the same reason. Any action taken by the court is independent of the action taken by DMV.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Your Hearing Rights · ¶1
text: You have the right to:

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Your Hearing Rights · item 1
text: Present relevant evidence and witnesses on your behalf.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Your Hearing Rights · item 2
text: Testify on your behalf or be represented by an attorney or other representative at your expense. Representation by an attorney is not required.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Your Hearing Rights · item 3
text: Review the evidence and cross examine the testimony of any witness. DMV bases its case only on written documents. If you wish to question someone who prepared a document or is listed on a document used as evidence, it is your responsibility to acquire a subpoena.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Your Hearing Rights · ¶2
text: For more information regarding Administrative Hearings, visit dmv.ca.gov/driversafety .

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Other Important Roadway Information › Unsafe Driver · ¶1
text: If you know someone who no longer drives safely, you may submit a Request for Driver Reexamination (DS 699) to DMV to review their driving qualifications. To obtain a form, visit dmv.ca.gov/reexamination .

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Record Confidentiality · ¶1
text: Most information in your driver’s record is available to the public, except physical or mental conditions, address, and social security number.

page_title: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Record Confidentiality · ¶2
text: You can get a copy of your driver’s record online or at a kiosk. For more information on record requests, visit dmv.ca.gov/record-requests .

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings · ¶1
text: To drive safely, you need to know what is around you. This helps you make good decisions and react to hazards on the road. This image shows the areas around your vehicle.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings · item 1
text: Green: Ahead of you.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings · item 2
text: Blue: Next to you.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings · item 3
text: Yellow: Blind spots.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings · item 4
text: Red: Behind you.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings · image
text: Image showing a driver's field of vision.
cap: Alt text: “Image showing a driver's field of vision.”

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Scan Your Surroundings · ¶1
text: To give yourself time to react, avoid last minute moves and hazards, always keep your eyes moving and scan the road at least 10 seconds ahead of your vehicle.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Tailgating (Following Too Closely) · ¶1
text: Tailgating makes it harder for you to see the road ahead because the vehicle in front of you blocks your view. You will not have enough time to react if the driver in front of you brakes suddenly. Use the three-second rule to ensure a safe following distance and avoid a collision. Following other vehicles at a safe distance gives you enough time to react if another driver makes a mistake.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Tailgating (Following Too Closely) · ¶2
text: If a vehicle merges in front of you too closely, take your foot off the accelerator. This creates space between you and the vehicle ahead.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Tailgating (Following Too Closely) · ¶3
text: Create more space in front of your vehicle when:

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Tailgating (Following Too Closely) · item 1
text: A tailgater is behind you. Maintain your course and speed. Then, when safe to do so, merge right to change into another lane and allow the tailgater to pass.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Tailgating (Following Too Closely) · item 2
text: Following motorcyclists on metal surfaces (bridge gratings, railroad tracks, etc.), and gravel.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is At Your Side · ¶1
path: Know What is At Your Side
text: Be aware of what is on each side of you. To maintain enough space to maneuver safely and react to other drivers:

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is At Your Side · item 1
path: Know What is At Your Side
text: Do not stay in another driver’s blind spot.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is At Your Side · item 2
path: Know What is At Your Side
text: Avoid driving directly alongside other vehicles.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is At Your Side · item 3
path: Know What is At Your Side
text: Make space for vehicles entering freeways, even if you have the right-of-way. Be ready for rapid changes and watch for signals from other drivers.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is At Your Side · item 4
path: Know What is At Your Side
text: Keep space between your vehicle and parked vehicles.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is At Your Side · item 5
path: Know What is At Your Side
text: Look both ways, even at intersections where traffic has a red light or stop sign.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · ¶1
text: Every vehicle has blind spots. These are areas around the vehicle that a driver cannot see when looking straight ahead or using the mirrors. For most vehicles, the blinds spots are at the sides, slightly behind the driver.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · ¶2
text: To check your blind spots, look over your right and left shoulders out of your side windows. Only turn your head when you look. Do not turn your whole body or steering wheel. Check your blind spots before you:

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · item 1
text: Change lanes.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · item 2
text: Turn at an intersection.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · item 3
text: Merge with traffic.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · item 4
text: Back up.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · item 5
text: Leave a parking space.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · item 6
text: Parallel park.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · item 7
text: Pull out from the curb.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · item 8
text: Open your car door.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · image
text: Image depicting a driver's blind spots.
cap: Alt text: “Image depicting a driver's blind spots.”

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · ¶3
text: The shaded areas are your blind spots

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is Behind You · ¶1
text: Knowing what is behind you can help you avoid rear-end collisions. Check traffic behind you often by using your rearview mirror, side mirrors, and turning your head when you:

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is Behind You · item 1
text: Change lanes.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is Behind You · item 2
text: Check your blind spots.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is Behind You · item 3
text: Reduce your speed.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is Behind You · item 4
text: Turn into a side road or driveway.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is Behind You · item 5
text: Stop to pull into a parking space.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is Behind You · item 6
text: Pull up to and away from the curb.

sec: Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is Behind You · item 7
text: Back up.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Darkness · ¶1
text: When driving at night, use your high-beam headlights on open country roads or dark city streets. Make sure you can stop in the distance lit by your headlights. Do not use high-beam headlights in areas where they are illegal. Dim your high-beam headlights to avoid blinding the driver of an oncoming vehicle. If another vehicle’s lights are too bright:

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Darkness · item 1
text: Do not look directly into the oncoming headlights.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Darkness · item 2
text: Look toward the right edge of your lane.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Darkness · item 3
text: Watch the oncoming vehicle out of the corner of your eye.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Darkness · item 4
text: Do not react to the other driver by keeping your high-beam headlights on. This only makes it harder for both of you to see.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Darkness · ¶2
text: When it is raining, use your low-beam headlights. Do not drive using only your parking lights. When you drive at night, remember:

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Darkness · item 5
text: Motorcycles, pedestrians, and bicyclists are much harder to see.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Darkness · item 6
text: Highway construction can take place at night. Reduce your speed in highway construction zones.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Darkness · item 7
text: When you leave a brightly lit place, drive slowly until your eyes adjust to the darkness.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Darkness · item 8
text: When a vehicle with one light drives toward you, drive as far to the right as possible. It could be a bicyclist, motorcyclist, or vehicle with a missing headlight.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Sun Glare · ¶1
text: To help manage sun glare:

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Sun Glare · item 1
text: Keep the inside and outside of your windshield clean.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Sun Glare · item 2
text: Wear polarized sunglasses.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Sun Glare · item 3
text: Maintain enough space between your vehicle and the vehicles around you.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Sun Glare · item 4
text: Make sure your car visor works and is free of anything that would restrict use.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Sun Glare · item 5
text: Be aware of pedestrians. You may have difficulty seeing them.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Sun Glare · item 6
text: Try to avoid driving during sunrise and sunset.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids · ¶1
text: A skid is when one or more of the tires lose traction with the road and the vehicle starts to slip. You may not be able to control your vehicle. There are a few different types of skids.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Slippery Surface Skids · ¶1
text: Ice and packed snow on the road can cause your vehicle to skid. This is even more likely if you are driving too fast or going downhill. Drive slowly and leave space between your vehicle and the vehicle ahead of you. To prevent skidding on slippery surfaces:

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Slippery Surface Skids · item 1
text: Slow down as you approach intersections and curves. For sharp curves, slow down as you approach and move through.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Slippery Surface Skids · item 2
text: Avoid fast turns and quick stops.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Slippery Surface Skids · item 3
text: Shift to low gear before going down a steep hill.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Slippery Surface Skids · item 4
text: Avoid areas like ice patches, wet leaves, oil, or standing water.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Slippery Surface Skids · ¶2
text: If you start to skid, follow these steps:

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Slippery Surface Skids · item 1
text: Slowly remove your foot from the accelerator

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Slippery Surface Skids · item 2
text: Do not use the brakes.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Slippery Surface Skids · item 3
text: Turn the steering wheel in the direction of the skid.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Slippery Surface Skids · item 4
text: Try to get a wheel on dry pavement.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · ¶1
text: A locked wheel skid is usually caused by braking too hard when you are going too fast. If this happens, your vehicle will skid no matter which way the steering wheel is turned. To get out of a locked wheel skid if your vehicle is equipped with:

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · item 1
text: Four-wheel antilock braking system (ABS), apply firm pressure on the brake pedal.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · item 2
text: Rear-wheel ABS (common in light trucks):

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · item 3
text: Ease up on the brake pedal while maintaining just enough pressure to allow the front wheels to roll again so you can steer.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · item 4
text: Stop braking and turn the steering wheel into the direction of the skid.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · item 5
text: Front-wheel ABS, remove your foot from the brake pedal to unlock the wheels. Steer in the direction you want to go and straighten the front wheels as the vehicle begins to straighten out.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · ¶2
text: Note To determine if your vehicle has ABS, refer to the vehicle owner’s manual.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · ¶3
text: If your vehicle is not equipped with ABS and begins to skid, quickly pump your brakes until you are at a safe speed. If you:

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · item 6
text: Press the brake pedal and it sinks to the floor, quickly pump the brakes by gently applying and releasing pressure on your brake pedal.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · item 7
text: Pump the brakes, down shift your vehicle into a lower or neutral gear to slow down. Then try using your emergency brake to stop.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · ¶4
text: If your brakes get wet, you can dry them by lightly pressing the accelerator and brake pedals at the same time. Only do this until the brakes dry.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · ¶1
text: Rain, snow, or mud can make the roads slippery. Drive more slowly than you would on a dry road and allow for more space between your vehicle and the vehicle ahead of you.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · ¶2
text: Adjust your speed for different conditions:

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · item 1
text: Wet road: Reduce your speed by 5 to 10 mph.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · item 2
text: Packed snow: Reduce your speed by half.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · item 3
text: Ice: Reduce your speed to no more than 5 mph.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · ¶3
text: Some road surfaces are more slippery than others when wet. These usually have warning signs posted. Here are situations where the road may be more slippery:

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · item 4
text: Shade from trees or buildings can hide icy spots on cold, wet days. These areas freeze first and dry out last.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · item 5
text: Bridges and overpasses tend to freeze before the rest of the road. They can have icy spots.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · item 6
text: When it starts to rain, the pavement can be very slippery.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · ¶4
text: Slow down at the first sign of rain, drizzle, or snow on the road. This is especially true if it has been dry and hot for some time, because oil and dust on the road’s surface have not been washed away.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · ¶5
text: Turn on your windshield wipers, low-beam headlights, and defroster. In a heavy rainstorm or snowstorm, you may not be able to see more than 100 feet in front of your vehicle. If you cannot see farther than 100 feet, it is not safe to drive faster than 30 mph. You may have to stop from time to time to wipe mud or snow off your windshield, headlights, and taillights. If you drive in snowy areas, carry snow chains for your tires. Snow chains give your tires more traction. Carry the correct number and type of chains for your vehicle.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Hydroplaning · ¶1
text: Hydroplaning occurs when driving in wet or rainy conditions. Hydroplaning is a vehicle riding on water because the tires lose all contact with the road. A slight change of direction, applying the brakes, or a gust of wind could throw the vehicle into a skid. To avoid hydroplaning:

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Hydroplaning · item 1
text: Drive slowly.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Hydroplaning · item 2
text: Steer around standing water, if possible.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Hydroplaning · item 3
text: Slow down if you hear sloshing sounds from the tires.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Hydroplaning · item 4
text: Slow down when changing lanes or direction.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Hydroplaning · ¶2
text: If your vehicle starts to hydroplane:

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Hydroplaning · item 5
text: Slow down gradually.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Hydroplaning · item 6
text: Do not use the brakes. Sudden braking may cause you to lose control of your vehicle.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Stuck in Snow or Mud · ¶1
text: If stuck in the snow or mud, follow these steps:

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Stuck in Snow or Mud · item 1
text: Shift into a low gear and keep the front wheels straight.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Stuck in Snow or Mud · item 2
text: Gently step on the accelerator. Avoid spinning the wheels.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Stuck in Snow or Mud · item 3
text: Drive slowly forward as far as possible.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Stuck in Snow or Mud · item 4
text: Shift into reverse and slowly back up as far as possible. Do not spin the wheels.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Stuck in Snow or Mud · item 5
text: Shift into a low gear again and drive forward.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Stuck in Snow or Mud · item 6
text: Repeat a forward-backward motion until the vehicle rolls free.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Stuck in Snow or Mud · item 7
text: In deep mud or snow, put boards, tree branches, etc., under the tires. Only take this action when the vehicle is stopped.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Flooded Roads · ¶1
text: Excessive water on a road may cause flooding. This can happen gradually or suddenly. It is important to understand the dangers of water on the road, including:

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Flooded Roads · item 1
text: Being swept off the road.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Flooded Roads · item 2
text: Floating debris and unseen hazards.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Flooded Roads · item 3
text: The road collapsing.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Flooded Roads · item 4
text: Vehicle malfunction.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Flooded Roads · item 5
text: Electrocution if there are fallen power lines.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Flooded Roads · ¶2
text: It may not be possible to determine the depth of the flood by looking. If the water is deep, the road may be too dangerous to cross. It is best to find another route. If you have no other option but to drive through a flooded road, drive slowly. After you make it through the water, test your brakes to make sure they work correctly.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › High Winds · ¶1
text: High winds can be a hazard while driving. This is especially true for larger vehicles such as trucks, campers, and vehicles with trailers. When driving in high winds:

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › High Winds · item 1
text: Reduce your speed. This gives you better control over your vehicle. You will have more time to react if your vehicle gets hit by a strong gust of wind.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › High Winds · item 2
text: Maintain a firm hand position on the steering wheel. Strong wind gusts are unpredictable. If you are not holding the wheel properly and a gust hits, you can lose control of the vehicle.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › High Winds · item 3
text: Be alert. Look ahead and watch for any debris on the road. Give yourself enough time to react to road hazards.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › High Winds · item 4
text: Do not use cruise control. Maintain maximum control of the accelerator if a gust occurs.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › High Winds · item 5
text: Be proactive. It may be safer to pull over and wait for the storm to pass.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · ¶1
text: It is best to avoid driving in heavy fog or smoke. Consider postponing your trip until the fog clears. If you must drive in heavy fog or smoke:

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · item 1
text: Drive slowly.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · item 2
text: Use your low-beam headlights. High-beam headlights will reflect back and cause glare.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · item 3
text: Never drive using only your parking or fog lights.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · item 4
text: Make sure you can stop within the space you can see ahead.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · item 5
text: Increase your following distance.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · item 6
text: Use your windshield wipers and defroster as necessary.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · item 7
text: Avoid crossing lanes or passing traffic unless absolutely necessary.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · item 8
text: Listen for traffic you cannot see.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · ¶2
text: If the fog becomes too thick to drive safely, consider pulling off the road. Activate your emergency flashers and wait for conditions to improve.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Law Enforcement Traffic Breaks · ¶1
text: During a traffic break, the officer turns on their emergency lights and slowly weaves across lanes. Law enforcement uses traffic breaks to:

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Law Enforcement Traffic Breaks · item 1
text: Slow or stop traffic to remove hazards from the road.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Law Enforcement Traffic Breaks · item 2
text: Slow or stop traffic during heavy fog or unusual traffic conditions.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Law Enforcement Traffic Breaks · item 3
text: Prevent collisions during unusual conditions.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Law Enforcement Traffic Breaks · ¶2
text: You should:

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Law Enforcement Traffic Breaks · item 4
text: Turn on your emergency flashers to warn other drivers.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Law Enforcement Traffic Breaks · item 5
text: Slowly decrease your speed to the same speed as the officer. Do not brake suddenly unless necessary to avoid a collision. Keep a safe distance from the patrol vehicle ahead of you.

sec: Understand the Road Conditions › Law Enforcement Traffic Breaks · item 6
text: Not drive past the patrol vehicle. Do not speed up until the officer turns off their emergency lights and traffic conditions allow you to return to your normal speed.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Seat Belts · ¶1
text: You and your passengers must wear seat belts. You can get a ticket if you do not. If your passenger is under 16 years old, you can also get a ticket if they are not wearing their seat belt.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Seat Belts · ¶2
text: Wearing the lap belt and shoulder harness of a seat belt will increase your chance of survival in most types of collisions. This image shows what can happen in a collision.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Seat Belts · ¶3
text: When you are in a collision, your vehicle stops. But you keep moving at the same speed you were traveling. You only stop when you hit the dashboard or windshield. If you are struck from the side, the impact could push you back and forth across the seat. Seat and shoulder belts keep you in a better position to control the vehicle. They may also minimize serious injuries.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Seat Belts · ¶4
text: It is important to wear the seat belt correctly to avoid injury or death:

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Seat Belts · item 1
text: Wear the shoulder harness across your shoulder and chest. There should be little to no slack. Do not wear the shoulder belt under your arm or behind your back.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Seat Belts · item 2
text: Adjust the lap belt so that it is snug and lies low across your hips. Otherwise you might slide out of the belt in a crash.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Seat Belts · item 3
text: If you are pregnant, wear the lap belt as low as possible under your abdomen. Place the shoulder strap between your breasts and to the side of your abdomen’s bulge.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Seat Belts · image
text: Image showing how your body would be thrown during an traffic collision.

text: IMPACT – If the red arrow were another car hitting your car on the driver’s side:

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Seat Belts · item 1
text: You would first be thrown against the driver’s side door,

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · ¶1
path: Child Restraint System and Safety Seats
text: You must secure children with a federally-approved child passenger restraint system or safety belt. The requirements depend on the child’s height and age.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · item 1
path: Child Restraint System and Safety Seats
text: Children who are under 2 years old, under 40 pounds, and under 3 feet 4 inches tall: Secure in a rear-facing child passenger restraint system.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · ¶2
path: Child Restraint System and Safety Seats
text: Note A child in a rear-facing child passenger restraint system may not ride in the front seat of an airbag-equipped vehicle.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · item 2
path: Child Restraint System and Safety Seats
text: Children who are under 8 years old, or who are less than 4 feet 9 inches tall: Secure in a child passenger restraint system in a rear seat. In some cases, children under 8 years old may ride in the front seat of a vehicle in a federally-approved child passenger restraint system. They may ride in the front seat if:

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · item 3
path: Child Restraint System and Safety Seats
text: There is no rear seat.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · item 4
path: Child Restraint System and Safety Seats
text: The rear seats are side-facing jump seats.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · item 5
path: Child Restraint System and Safety Seats
text: The rear seats are rear-facing seats.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · item 6
path: Child Restraint System and Safety Seats
text: The child passenger restraint system cannot be installed properly in the rear seat.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · item 7
path: Child Restraint System and Safety Seats
text: All rear seats are already occupied by children 7 years old or younger.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · item 8
path: Child Restraint System and Safety Seats
text: Medical reasons prevent the child from riding in the back seat.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · item 9
path: Child Restraint System and Safety Seats
text: Children who are 8 years old or older, or at least 4 feet 9 inches tall: May use a properly secured safety belt that meets federal standards.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · ¶3
path: Child Restraint System and Safety Seats
text: Your local law enforcement agency or fire department can check the installation of your child passenger restraint system. As your child grows, check that the child passenger restraint system is the right size.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Air Bags · ¶1
text: Air bags are a valuable safety feature on many vehicles. They can help keep you safer than a seat belt alone.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Air Bags · ¶2
text: Ride at least 10 inches from the airbag cover, as long as you can maintain full control of your vehicle. Measure from the center of the steering wheel to your breastbone. Contact your vehicle dealer or manufacturer if you cannot safely sit 10 inches away from the air bag. They may have advice about additional ways to move back from your air bag. Passengers should also sit at least 10 inches away from the passenger-side air bag.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Air Bags · ¶3
text: Note Children seated next to a side air bag may be at risk of serious or fatal injury.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Unattended Children and Pets · ¶1
text: It is illegal to leave a child who is six years old or younger unattended in a vehicle. A child may be left under the supervision of a person who is at least 12 years old.

sec: Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Unattended Children and Pets · ¶2
text: It is dangerous and illegal to leave children or animals in a hot vehicle. The temperature inside a parked vehicle can rise rapidly when it is sitting in the sun. This is true even if a window is left slightly open. Too much exposure to heat can lead to dehydration, heat stroke, and death.

sec: Manage Your Speed · ¶1
text: In California, you may never drive faster than is safe for the current road conditions. This is known as the Basic Speed Law.

sec: Manage Your Speed · ¶2
text: Make sure you manage your speed and slow down when conditions call for it. Regardless of the posted speed limit, your speed should depend on:

sec: Manage Your Speed · item 1
text: The number of vehicles on the road.

sec: Manage Your Speed · item 2
text: The speed of other vehicles on the road.

sec: Manage Your Speed · item 3
text: The road surface: smooth, rough, graveled, wet, dry, wide, or narrow.

sec: Manage Your Speed · item 4
text: Bicyclists or pedestrians on or crossing the road.

sec: Manage Your Speed · item 5
text: Weather: rain, fog, snow, wind, or dust.

sec: Manage Your Speed · item 6
text: Traffic congestion: small changes in your driving habits can help reduce congestion. Avoid weaving in and out of freeway lanes.

sec: Manage Your Speed · ¶3
text: There are also situations with specific speed limit laws and conditions where you should reduce your speed. Unless otherwise posted, the ideal maximum speed limit on most California highways is 65 mph. It is 55 mph on a two-lane undivided highway and for vehicles towing trailers.

sec: Choose Between Hazards · ¶1
text: Sometimes dangers will be on both sides of the road at the same time. For example, parked cars to the right and oncoming cars to the left.

sec: Choose Between Hazards · ¶2
text: If one danger is greater than the other, give more space to the most dangerous situation. Suppose you are on a two-lane road with an oncoming vehicle to the left and a bicyclist ahead to your right. Instead of driving between the vehicle and the bicyclist, take one danger at a time. Slow down and let the oncoming vehicle pass. When the vehicle has passed, move to the left to allow plenty of space (at least three feet) to pass the bicyclist. If there is a steady flow of oncoming vehicles, use as much of the left lane as you safely can to pass the bicyclist.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies · ¶1
text: There are many types of emergencies you may encounter when you drive. Knowing how to handle emergencies can help keep you safe.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Tire Blowout · ¶1
text: If you have a tire blowout, do not panic or overreact. Suddenly braking or abruptly removing your foot from the accelerator can result in a loss of control over the vehicle. Instead, you should take the following steps recommended by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration:

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Tire Blowout · item 1
text: Hold the steering wheel with both hands.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Tire Blowout · item 2
text: Maintain your vehicle speed if possible and safe.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Tire Blowout · item 3
text: Gradually release the accelerator.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Tire Blowout · item 4
text: Correct the steering as necessary to stabilize your vehicle and regain control.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Tire Blowout · item 5
text: Look and steer in the direction you want your vehicle to go.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Tire Blowout · item 6
text: Once your vehicle has stabilized, continue to slow down and pull off the road where and when it’s safe.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Driving Off the Pavement · ¶1
text: If your wheels drift off the pavement:

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Driving Off the Pavement · item 1
text: Grip the steering wheel firmly.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Driving Off the Pavement · item 2
text: Remove your foot from the accelerator.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Driving Off the Pavement · item 3
text: Brake gently.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Driving Off the Pavement · item 4
text: Check for traffic behind you.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Driving Off the Pavement · item 5
text: Carefully steer back onto the pavement.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Driving Off the Pavement · ¶2
text: Do not pull or turn your steering wheel with too much force. This may cause you to drive into oncoming traffic.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Overheating Conditions · ¶1
text: In extreme heat, you should:

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Overheating Conditions · item 1
text: Watch the temperature gauge.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Overheating Conditions · item 2
text: Avoid driving at high speeds for long periods.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Overheating Conditions · item 3
text: Turn off the air conditioner.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Overheating Conditions · ¶2
text: In extreme cold, you should:

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Overheating Conditions · item 4
text: Watch the temperature gauge. The engine may not have the correct level of antifreeze.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Overheating Conditions · item 5
text: Use the defroster or slightly open your windows to keep them from fogging up.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Overheating Conditions · ¶3
text: Note See the vehicle owner’s manual for more information.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · ¶1
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
text: If your vehicle stops working on the freeway:

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · item 1
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
text: Safely pull over to the right shoulder.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · item 2
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
text: Exit on the right side so you are away from traffic if you must get out of the vehicle.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · item 3
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
text: Dial 511 from your cell phone or locate call box for assistance..

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · item 4
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
text: Return to your vehicle as soon as you can. Get back into the vehicle from the right side (away from traffic).

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · item 5
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
text: Stay inside your vehicle with your seat belt on until help arrives.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · item 6
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
text: Use your emergency flashers at your discretion. They can help other vehicles see you at night and in different weather conditions.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · ¶2
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
text: There are certain circumstances where it is safer to get out of your vehicle and stay away. These include situations where there is:

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · item 1
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
text: Not enough space on the shoulder.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · item 2
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
text: A guardrail.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · item 3
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
text: An area for you to safely stay away from freeway lanes.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · ¶1
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP)
text: During commute times, the CHP FSP provides free emergency roadside services in certain areas. If you get stuck on the freeway because your vehicle stops running, FSP will:

path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP)
text: Provide a gallon of gas if you run out.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · item 2
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP)
text: Jump start your vehicle if the battery is dead.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · item 3
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP)
text: Refill your radiator and tape hoses.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · item 4
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP)
text: Change a flat tire.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · item 5
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP)
text: Report a collision to CHP.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · ¶2
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP)
text: If FSP cannot start your vehicle, they will have it towed (free of charge) to a CHP-approved location. CHP will notify an auto club or towing service.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · ¶3
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP)
text: FSP will not:

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · item 6
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP)
text: Tow your vehicle to a private repair service or residence.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · item 7
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP)
text: Recommend tow service companies or repair and body shops.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · item 8
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP)
text: Tow motorcycles.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · item 9
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP)
text: Help vehicles which have been involved in a collision, unless they are directed to by CHP.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · ¶4
path: If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway
California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP)
text: Call 511 for FSP information and assistance.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Disabled Vehicles on Railroad Tracks · ¶1
text: If your vehicle stalls or stops while blocking part of a train track with a train approaching and warning lights flashing:

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Disabled Vehicles on Railroad Tracks · item 1
text: Immediately exit your vehicle. Run away from the tracks diagonally in the direction the train is coming from. Then call 911.

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Disabled Vehicles on Railroad Tracks · ¶2
text: If you do not see a train approaching and warning lights are not flashing:

sec: Know How to Handle Emergencies › Disabled Vehicles on Railroad Tracks · item 2
text: Exit your vehicle. Dial the number located on the railroad crossing posts or metal control box near the tracks. Provide the crossing number (if posted). Tell them a vehicle is on the tracks. Then call 911.
