sec: Do Not Drive Distracted · ¶1
text: Avoid distractions while you drive. Some common distractions are:

sec: Do Not Drive Distracted · item 1
text: Looking at a phone, navigation system, children, and pets.

sec: Do Not Drive Distracted · item 2
text: Changing music or volume.

sec: Do Not Drive Distracted · item 3
text: Applying makeup or shaving.

sec: Cell Phones and Texting · ¶1
text: Cell phones are the main source of distracted driving. Driving while using a handheld cell phone is unsafe and illegal.

sec: Cell Phones and Texting · ¶2
text: Adult drivers should only use a cell phone in hands-free mode when necessary.

sec: Cell Phones and Texting · item 1
text: Do not answer your cell phone if it rings. Let the call go to voicemail. If you must return or make a call, pull safely off the road.

sec: Cell Phones and Texting · item 2
text: Do not send or read text messages or emails while driving.

sec: Cell Phones and Texting · item 3
text: Mount your cell phone on the windshield, dashboard, or center console. It cannot block your view of the road.

sec: Cell Phones and Texting · item 4
text: Use the single swipe or touch feature on the mounted cell phone.

sec: Minors And Cell Phones · ¶1
text: It is against the law for a minor to use a cell phone or electronic wireless device to answer calls and send or respond to text messages while driving.

sec: Minors And Cell Phones · ¶2
text: EXCEPTION : Minors may use a cell phone to make a call for emergency assistance.

sec: Be Familiar with New Technology · ¶1
text: The technology in vehicles is always advancing. We will see more self-driving vehicles and vehicles with advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) on the road. Vehicles with these systems may respond to road situations differently than a human driver would.

sec: Be Aware of Carbon Monoxide · ¶1
text: All gas-powered vehicles produce carbon monoxide. Carbon monoxide is a deadly odorless gas released from a vehicle’s exhaust pipe. Never start your vehicle inside the garage with the door closed. Symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning include:

sec: Be Aware of Carbon Monoxide · item 1
text: Tiredness

sec: Be Aware of Carbon Monoxide · item 2
text: Yawning

sec: Be Aware of Carbon Monoxide · item 3
text: Dizziness

sec: Be Aware of Carbon Monoxide · item 4
text: Nausea

sec: Be Aware of Carbon Monoxide · item 5
text: Headache

sec: Be Aware of Carbon Monoxide · item 6
text: Ringing in the ears

sec: Be Aware of Carbon Monoxide · ¶2
text: If you are experiencing any of these symptoms, have your exhaust system checked.

sec: Intro · ¶1
text: California’s driving under the influence (DUI) laws apply to both alcohol and drugs. It is illegal to drive while under the influence of alcohol or any drug that affects your ability to drive safely. As you age, your tolerance to alcohol decreases, which increases the risk of alcohol-related driving problems. The law does not see a difference between illegal drugs and medications you get from a doctor or pharmacy. They can all affect your ability to drive safely and react to what you see and hear.

sec: Intro · ¶2
text: No matter what age you are, it is illegal to drive after:

sec: Intro · item 1
text: Drinking excessive amounts of alcohol in any form. This includes medications like cough syrup.

sec: Intro · item 2
text: Taking any drug that affects your ability to drive. This includes prescriptions or over-the-counter medications.

sec: Intro · item 3
text: Using any combination of alcohol or drugs that decreases your ability to drive safely.

sec: Intro · ¶3
text: Make sure you read medication labels and know the effects of any drug you use. If a law enforcement officer thinks you are driving while under the influence of drugs or alcohol, they have the right to ask you to take a blood or urine test. If you refuse to take one, DMV will suspend or revoke your driving privilege for one year.

sec: Intro · ¶4
text: Important If you are 13 to 20 years old and convicted of operating a bicycle while under the influence of alcohol or drugs, your driving privilege may be suspended or delayed for one year once you are eligible to drive.

sec: Use or Possession of Alcohol or Cannabis Products in a Vehicle · ¶1
path: Use or Possession of Alcohol or Cannabis Products in a Vehicle
text: The law is very strict about carrying alcohol or cannabis products in your vehicle with you. It is illegal to drink any alcohol, to smoke or eat a cannabis product while you are driving or riding as a passenger in a vehicle. If you are carrying any alcohol or cannabis in your vehicle, the container must be sealed and unopened. If it is open, you must keep the container in the trunk or place where passengers do not sit. It is also illegal to keep an open container of alcohol in your glove box. This law does not apply if you are a passenger in a bus, taxi, camper, or motorhome.

sec: Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · ¶1
text: When you consume alcohol, traces of it enter your bloodstream. Your BAC measures how much alcohol is present in your bloodstream.

sec: Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · ¶2
text: It is illegal for you to drive if you have a BAC of:

sec: Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · item 1
text: 0.08% or higher if you are over 21 years old.

sec: Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · item 2
text: 0.01% or higher if you are under 21 years old.

sec: Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · item 3
text: 0.01% or higher at any age if you are on DUI probation.

sec: Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · item 4
text: 0.04% or higher if you drive a vehicle that requires a commercial driver’s license.

sec: Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · item 5
text: 0.04% or higher if you are driving a passenger for hire.

sec: Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · ¶3
text: If you drive with an illegal BAC, a law enforcement officer can charge you with DUI. Even if your BAC is below legal limits, that does not mean it is safe for you to drive. Almost everyone feels negative effects of alcohol, even at levels lower than the legal limit. Depending on how badly you are impaired, you may be arrested and convicted of a DUI even without a BAC measurement.

sec: Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · ¶4
text: The table below shows BAC estimates based on how many drinks are consumed, gender, and body weight. Remember, even one drink can affect your ability to drive safely.

text: Table displaying Blood Alcohol Concentration estimates based on how many drinks are consumed, gender, and body weight.

sec: Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · ¶5
text: Note It is illegal to drink alcohol or take drugs when you are operating a boat, jet ski, water skis, aquaplane, or similar vessels. Learn more in the California Harbors and Navigation Code .

sec: DUI Arrests · ¶1
text: When you drive in California, you consent to a breath, blood, or urine test if a law enforcement officer suspects you of DUI. If you agreed to take a preliminary alcohol screening (PAS) or breath test, you may still be required to take a blood or urine test to detect the presence of drugs. If you refuse, DMV will suspend or revoke your driving privilege. If you are arrested for DUI:

sec: DUI Arrests · item 1
text: California’s Administrative Per Se law requires DMV to suspend your driving privilege.

sec: DUI Arrests · item 2
text: The law enforcement officer may take your driver’s license and give you a temporary driver’s license for 30 days.

sec: DUI Arrests · item 3
text: You may request a DMV administrative hearing within 10 days from the date of your arrest.

sec: DUI Convictions · ¶1
text: If you are convicted of a DUI, DMV will suspend or revoke your driving privilege and you:

sec: DUI Convictions · item 1
text: Must complete a DUI program.

sec: DUI Convictions · item 2
text: Must file a California Insurance Proof Certificate (SR 22/SR 1P).

sec: DUI Convictions · item 3
text: Must pay any applicable license reissue or restriction fees.

sec: DUI Convictions · item 4
text: May be required to install an ignition interlock device (IID) on your vehicle.

sec: DUI Convictions · ¶2
text: Here are some additional penalties if you are convicted of DUI:

sec: DUI Convictions · item 5
text: You may be sentenced to up to six months in jail.

sec: DUI Convictions · item 6
text: You may have to pay a fine.

sec: DUI Convictions · item 7
text: Law enforcement may impound your vehicle and you may have to pay a storage fee.

sec: DUI Convictions · item 8
text: If you cause serious injury or death while driving under the influence of drugs or alcohol, you may face civil lawsuits.

sec: DUI Convictions · ¶3
text: All DUI convictions remain on your driver’s record for 10 years. If you get any other DUIs during that time, the court or DMV may give you an additional penalty.

sec: Drivers Under 21 · ¶1
text: If you are under 21 years old, there are additional laws for possessing and consuming alcohol.

sec: Drivers Under 21 › Possessing alcohol: · item 1
text: You may not carry any alcohol beverage inside a vehicle unless an individual who is 21 years old or older is with you. The container must be full, sealed, and unopened. If opened, the alcohol must be kept in the trunk or place where passengers do not sit. Exception : If you are working for someone with an off-site liquor sales license, you may carry alcoholic beverages in closed containers.

sec: Drivers Under 21 › Possessing alcohol: · item 2
text: If you are caught with alcohol in your vehicle, law enforcement can impound your vehicle for up to 30 days. The court may fine you and suspend your driver’s license for one year. If you do not already have a driver’s license, the court may ask DMV to delay giving you your first driver’s license for up to one year.

sec: Drivers Under 21 › Consuming alcohol: · item 1
text: If a law enforcement officer suspects you of consuming alcohol, they can require you to take a hand-held breath test, PAS, or another chemical test.

sec: Drivers Under 21 › Consuming alcohol: · item 2
text: If you are convicted of a DUI with a BAC of 0.01% or higher, DMV may revoke your driving privilege for one year. You must also complete a licensed DUI program.

sec: Drivers Under 21 › Consuming alcohol: · item 3
text: If your PAS shows a BAC of 0.05% or higher, the officer may require you to take a breath or blood test.

sec: Drivers Under 21 › Consuming alcohol: · item 4
text: If a later test shows you have a BAC of 0.05% or higher, you may be arrested for a DUI and your driving privilege may be suspended.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Intro · ¶1
text: You must have your proof of financial responsibility (insurance) when you drive and for a drive test. If you get into a collision, you must show proof to the other drivers involved in the collision.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Insurance Requirements · ¶1
text: Your insurance must cover at least:

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Insurance Requirements · item 1
text: $30,000 for a single death or injury.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Insurance Requirements · item 2
text: $60,000 for death or injury to more than one person.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Insurance Requirements · item 3
text: $15,000 for property damage.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Insurance Requirements · ¶2
text: Parents or guardians take on financial responsibility for drivers younger than 18 years old and pay for damages if the driver is involved in a collision. Drivers who are 18 years old and older take on their own financial responsibility.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Insurance Requirements · ¶3
text: Before you buy insurance, make sure that the agent, broker, or insurance provider is licensed by the California Department of Insurance. For more information, visit insurance.ca.gov/license-status/ .

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Driving Without Insurance · ¶1
text: Your driving privilege will be suspended for up to four years if you are in a collision and do not have proper insurance coverage. It does not matter who was at fault.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Driving Without Insurance · ¶2
text: You can get your driver’s license back during the last three years of the suspension if you provide a California Insurance Proof Certificate (SR 22/SR 1P) and maintain it during the three-year period.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Low-cost Insurance · ¶1
text: If you cannot afford liability insurance, you may be eligible for the California Low Cost Automobile Insurance Program. For more information, visit mylowcostauto.com or call 1-866-602-8861.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions · ¶1
text: Understand factors that lead to collisions so you can try to avoid them.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › Causes of Collisions · ¶1
text: The most common causes of collisions are:

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › Causes of Collisions · item 1
text: Driver distractions.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › Causes of Collisions · item 2
text: Unsafe speed.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › Causes of Collisions · item 3
text: Improper turns.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › Causes of Collisions · item 4
text: Not following the right-of-way rules.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › Causes of Collisions · item 5
text: Not following stop signals and signs.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › Causes of Collisions · item 6
text: Driving on the wrong side of the road.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › Causes of Collisions · item 7
text: A vehicle traveling faster or slower than the flow of traffic.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › Causes of Collisions · ¶2
text: If you see a vehicle’s emergency flashers ahead, slow down. There may be a collision or other road emergency. Pass carefully.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › Causes of Collisions · ¶3
text: Avoid driving near collisions, if possible. If anyone is injured, they will get help faster if other vehicles are not blocking the road.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › What to Do if You Are in a Collision · item 1
path: What to Do if You Are in a Collision
text: If you are in a collision:

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › What to Do if You Are in a Collision · item 2
path: What to Do if You Are in a Collision
text: You must stop. Someone could be injured and need your help. Failing to stop or leaving the scene of an accident is called a hit-and-run. The punishment is severe if you are convicted of a hit-and-run.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › What to Do if You Are in a Collision · item 3
path: What to Do if You Are in a Collision
text: Call 911 right away if anyone is hurt.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › What to Do if You Are in a Collision · item 4
path: What to Do if You Are in a Collision
text: Move your vehicle out of traffic if no one is hurt. Then call 911.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › What to Do if You Are in a Collision · item 5
path: What to Do if You Are in a Collision
text: Show your driver’s license, vehicle registration card, insurance information, and current address to the other driver, law enforcement officer, and anyone else involved in the collision.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › What to Do if You Are in a Collision · item 6
path: What to Do if You Are in a Collision
text: You must make a report to law enforcement within 24 hours of the collision if anyone is injured or killed. Your insurance agent, broker, or legal representative can also file the report.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › What to Do if You Are in a Collision · item 7
path: What to Do if You Are in a Collision
text: Try to find the owner if your vehicle hits or rolls into a parked car or other property. If you cannot find the owner, leave a note with your name, phone number, and address. Securely attach the note to the vehicle or property. Report the collision to law enforcement.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › What to Do if You Are in a Collision · item 8
path: What to Do if You Are in a Collision
text: If you kill or injure an animal, call the nearest humane society or law enforcement. Do not try to move an injured animal.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › Reporting a Collision · ¶1
text: If you are in a collision, you must report it to DMV within 10 days if:

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › Reporting a Collision · item 1
text: The collision caused more than $1,000 in damage to property.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › Reporting a Collision · item 2
text: Anyone was injured or killed. This applies even if the injuries were minor.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › Reporting a Collision · ¶2
text: Each driver must file a Report of Traffic Accident Occurring in California (SR 1) with DMV at dmv.ca.gov/accidentreport . You (or your representative) must file a report whether or not you caused the collision. This applies even if the collision happened on private property.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions › Reporting a Collision · ¶3
text: Your driving privilege will be suspended if you fail to file a report. Law enforcement will not make a report for you.

page_title: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions
sec: Collisions on Your Driver’s Record · ¶1
text: If you are involved in a collision resulting in $1,000 in damage, or where anyone is injured or dies, it is your responsibility to report the collision to DMV. DMV will add it to your driver’s record. It does not matter who caused the collision.

sec: Intro · ¶1
text: You need to register your vehicle in California to use it in the state. For more information, visit dmv.ca.gov/vrservices .

sec: Buying or Selling a Vehicle · ¶1
text: When you buy a vehicle, you have 10 days to transfer ownership to your name.

sec: Buying or Selling a Vehicle · ¶2
text: When you sell a vehicle, you must notify DMV within five days by completing a Notice of Transfer and Release of Liability at dmv.ca.gov/nrl .

sec: Out-of-State Vehicles · ¶1
text: You have 20 days to register your vehicle after you become a resident or get a job in California. For more information, visit dmv.ca.gov/outofstatevr .

sec: Out-of-State Vehicles · ¶2
text: All vehicles registered in California are required to meet California requirements including vehicle emission controls in support of California’s clean air standards. DMV cannot register a vehicle if it does not qualify.

sec: Intro · ¶1
text: Eventually, every driver will need to evaluate and assess their driving skills and abilities. If you are concerned about your driving, ask a trusted driver with a valid driver’s license to sit in the passenger seat and observe your driving. Your observer should note any dangerous driving behaviors and give suggestions for improvement. Listen carefully and apply what you have learned. Consider professional driving lessons or driving classes as an alternative.

sec: Reexamination · ¶1
text: The Vehicle Code allows DMV to investigate and reexamine every driver’s ability to operate a motor vehicle safely. A physical or mental condition or poor driver’s record can be the basis for a reexamination, not a driver’s age. Drivers with a physical or mental condition can be referred to DMV by a physician, law enforcement, or family member by submitting a completed Request for Driver Reexamination (DS 699) form.

sec: Reexamination · ¶2
text: Cognitive disorders, such as dementia, seizure disorder, brain tumor, Parkinson’s disease, stroke, or vertigo, present a significant challenge to safe driving. Individuals suffering from these conditions may lose their ability to drive safely.

sec: Reexamination · ¶3
text: Note When a referral or diagnosis for a driver with a mild cognitive impairment is received by DMV, the Driver Safety team will schedule a reexamination. For more information regarding the reexamination process, visit dmv.ca.gov/reexamination .

sec: Reexamination · ¶4
text: DMV may do the following:

sec: Reexamination · item 1
text: Request medical information from you or your physician.

sec: Reexamination · item 2
text: Conduct an in-person or over the telephone reexamination.

sec: Reexamination · item 3
text: Require you to take a knowledge, vision, or driving test(s).

sec: Reexamination · item 4
text: Issue you a limited term driver’s license.

sec: Reexamination · item 5
text: Immediately suspend or revoke your driving privilege if your physical or mental condition presents an immediate threat to public safety.

sec: Reexamination · item 6
text: Take no action against your driving privilege.

sec: Priority Reexamination · ¶1
text: If you come in contact with law enforcement and receive a Notice of Priority Reexamination of Driver with a check mark in the top box, carefully read the form. You have five working days to contact DMV to initiate the process or your driving privilege will be automatically suspended.

sec: Driver’s License Restrictions · ¶1
text: DMV places restrictions on a driver’s license to ensure a driver is operating a vehicle within their ability. Restrictions may be imposed by DMV or required by law. Restrictions placed on your driving privilege will be reasonable and necessary for your safety and the safety of others. Restrictions and conditions may include:

sec: Driver’s License Restrictions · item 1
text: Requiring a driver to place special mechanical devices on their vehicle, such as hand controls.

sec: Driver’s License Restrictions · item 2
text: Limiting when and where a person may drive, such as no night or freeway driving.

sec: Driver’s License Restrictions · item 3
text: Requiring eyeglasses or corrective contact lenses.

sec: Driver’s License Restrictions · item 4
text: Requiring additional devices, such as outside mirrors.

sec: Driver’s License Restrictions · ¶2
text: Note There are no specific restrictions for seniors. All restrictions are based on conditions, not age.

sec: Driver’s License Restrictions · ¶3
text: Any restriction placed on your driver’s license is based on the examiner’s findings and recommendations.

sec: Intro · ¶1
text: Senior drivers often have unique needs and concerns about driving. Driving requires certain physical, visual, and mental abilities. We all want to continue driving as long as we can. However, the time may come when we must limit or stop driving temporarily or permanently. Here are some warning signs of an unsafe driver:

sec: Intro · item 1
text: Getting lost in familiar places.

sec: Intro · item 2
text: Dents and scrapes on the car, fences, mailbox, garage doors, etc.

sec: Intro · item 3
text: Frequent close calls or collisions.

sec: Intro · ¶2
text: Senior drivers may consider:

sec: Intro · item 4
text: Limiting or not driving at night.

sec: Intro · item 5
text: If night driving is necessary, choose a well-lit route.

sec: Intro · item 6
text: Driving during the time of day when traffic is light.

sec: Intro · item 7
text: Avoiding difficult intersections.

sec: Intro · item 8
text: Driving for short distances or limiting driving to essential places.

sec: Intro · item 9
text: No freeway driving.

sec: Intro · item 10
text: Installing an additional right-side mirror.

sec: Intro · ¶3
text: To get the Driver Skills Self-Assessment Questionnaire, visit dmv.ca.gov/driver-skills .

sec: Driver’s License Renewal · ¶1
text: If you are 70 years old or older at the time your driver’s license expires, you are required to renew your driver’s license in person and pass a vision test. In some cases, other exams may be required. If a knowledge test is required, you may be eligible to select “eLearning” when completing your application online. DMV sends a renewal notice to your address of record about 90 days before your driver’s license expires. If you do not receive a renewal notice, complete a Driver License or Identification Card Application at dmv.ca.gov/dlservices or at a DMV office. Visit dmv.ca.gov/driver-ed for more information and sample tests.

sec: DMV’s Community Liaison and Outreach · ¶1
text: The Community Liaison’s primary function is to represent public safety interests for all Californians, with a focus in addressing the concerns of senior drivers and teens. The liaison can assist as a go-between to ensure drivers are treated fairly, consistently with laws and regulations, and with dignity and respect. While the Community Liaison cannot represent you in a DMV hearing or reexamination, they can provide you with useful tools and information.

sec: DMV’s Community Liaison and Outreach · ¶2
text: For information about outreach services in your area or to speak to a liaison, contact Community Liaison and Outreach at (833) 493-0675.

sec: Cognitive Impairment · ¶1
text: Seniors suffering from dementia present a significant challenge to safe driving. Individuals with progressive dementia ultimately lose their ability to drive safely. It is often up to caregivers, physicians, and law enforcement, to stop these seniors from driving and arrange alternative transportation. For more information about the reexamination process, visit dmv.ca.gov/reexamination .

sec: Mature Driver Program · ¶1
text: The Mature Driver Improvement Program is an eight-hour course for drivers 55 years old and older. It covers a range of topics that are of special interest to mature drivers.

sec: Mature Driver Program · ¶2
text: Your insurance company may offer discounts if you complete the program. Contact your insurance provider with a copy of your completion certificate. Your certificate is valid for three years. You can renew it by completing another four-hour course.

sec: Mature Driver Program · ¶3
text: You can take the course through DMV-approved providers. Visit dmv.ca.gov/seniors for more information, including locations near you.

sec: Senior ID Cards · ¶1
text: If you are 62 years old or older, you are eligible for a no-fee Senior ID card. Drivers of any age who are unable to continue driving safely due to a physical or mental condition may be eligible to exchange their driver’s license for a no-fee ID card. The ID card serves as identification only. Details may be found at dmv.ca.gov/id-cards .

sec: Intro · row 1
text: Behind-the-wheel drive test | A drive test where you have control of the vehicle and are accompanied by a DMV examiner who is evaluating your driving skills.

sec: Intro · row 2
text: Blood alcohol concentration (BAC) | Your BAC is the amount of alcohol in your blood. For example, if your BAC is 0.10%, that means you have 0.10 grams of alcohol in 100 milliliters of blood.

sec: Intro · row 3
text: Driving performance evaluation (DPE) | DPE is the portion of the behind-the-wheel drive test when you drive your car with a DMV examiner who evaluates your driving skills.

sec: Intro · row 4
text: Pedestrian | A pedestrian is a person walking and can also be a person with a disability using a tricycle, quadricycle, or wheelchair for transportation.

sec: Intro · row 5
text: Right-of-way | Helps determine who is allowed to go first in situations where vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists meet on the road.

sec: Intro · row 6
text: Three-second rule | A driving rule that helps you estimate how closely you should follow other vehicles. When the vehicle in front of you passes a certain point, such as a sign, count three seconds. If you pass the same point before you finish counting, you are following too closely.

sec: Intro · row 7
text: Traffic citation | Also known as a ticket, a traffic citation is an official summons issued by law enforcement for violating a traffic law.

sec: Intro · row 8
text: Vulnerable road users (VRU) | VRUs are non-motorized road users, such as cyclists, pedestrians, and persons with disabilities or reduced mobility and orientation using a wheelchair, tricycle, or quadricycle.

sec: Intro · row 9
text: Yield | Yield means to wait for, slow down, and be ready to stop (if necessary) to allow other vehicles or pedestrians who have right-of-way to proceed.
